sentences: The entertainment industry makes the modern world's mirth luminous.
Entertainment provides people to experience and process emotions that ordinary life may not provide opportunities for.
Be it emotional nourishment or a social knot, a person's right to entertainment is uncontroverted.
For people with disabilities, this right remains elusive.

While Indian law acknowledges and recognises the reinforcement of accessibility of entertainment to people with disabilities, it fails to unveil the differentiation between physical accessibility and entertainment accessibility.

The aspect of physical accessibility is grounded in the legal foundation of the RPwD Act, but the absence of any nationwide comprehensive data itself demonstrates the difficulty of examining the disability accessibility of the Indian entertainment industry.

Even though the RPwD Act mandates accessibility to public places such as theatres, data by INOX Cinema subsequently suggest that only 63 per cent of Indian cinemas have infrastructure viable for access by persons with disabilities.

For instance, in the Golukam cinema case, Suresh, a person with a 60% locomotor disability, was forced to climb a staircase to a second-floor screen because the newly built complex had no lift or ramp.
There exists no single regulatory framework governing the entertainment industry.
Isolated frameworks subsist for different forms of distinguished entertainment, thus access to entertainment being contingent on the medium through which it is consumed.
The Rights of Persons with Disabilities disembark in outlining the void left by such statutory ambiguity.

Sections 29 and 30 recognise the participation of persons with disabilities in cultural, recreational and sporting activity, while sections 40 and 42 address accessibility standards, access to information and compliance with accessibility requirements.
The quagmire exist in translate this overarching statutory commitment into consistent and enforceable obligations across different segments of the entertainment industry.

While Cinema halls are regulated under the Cinematograph Act, the Streaming platforms fall within the regulatory framework administered by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting under the Information Technology Rules.

The Sporting venues are governed by their respective sports bodies and venue-specific regulations while Cultural and religious establishments are subject to a combination of general accessibility law, local regulation, and the rules of their managing authorities.
The fragmentation becomes conspicuous in its implementation.
Yash Raj Films, the matter pertained to the accessibility of films for persons with visual and hearing impairments.
The Delhi High Court directed the Ministry to formulate mandatory accessibility standards.

Following this, the Ministry notified guidelines on accessibility of OTT content for persons with hearing and visual impairments, requiring newly published content to carry captioning or Indian Sign Language interpretation and audio description within a phased implementation schedule.

Yet these guidelines notably prescribe no penalty or consequence for non-compliance once the implementation period lapses, nor any repercussion for a publisher's failure to submit the periodic conformance reports the guidelines themselves require.
The continuing difficulties faced by persons with disabilities illustrate the implementation problem.

Mythri Movie Makers, proceedings before the Delhi High Court concerning the inaccessible release of Pushpa 2: The Rule raised concern about the films continuing to be exhibited without accessibility features on a universal basis, and that even where such features exist, they are restricted to a limited number of screenings governed by a booking process that is itself inaccessible.
The Court has since treated the grievance as extending beyond a single film to the broader question of accessibility in cinema, directing stakeholders to arrive at a workable resolution.
That this litigation became necessary within two years of the 2024 guidelines being issued illustrates precisely how standards without an enforcement backbone fail to translate into practice.
Sporting venues identify a similar gap through a distinct mechanism.

In January 2023, two visually impaired spectators were stopped from entering Holkar Stadium in Indore because their accompanying aides did not possess separate tickets, and were allowed entry only after intervention by senior police officials, rather than as a matter of established right.
Cultural and religious spaces demonstrate the same difficulty.

In 2017, a wheelchair user was denied entry to Goa's Mangueshi Temple because her wheelchair was treated as a "vehicle," an incident that required intervention by disability rights groups rather than resolution through any existing regulatory channel.
These incidents arise under different legal and institutional regimes, yet they reveal a common structural problem:
accessibility is addressed only after exclusion has occurred, and the remedy depends on an individual's ability to complain, litigate, or secure institutional intervention.
The central issue, therefore, is not whether Indian law recognises accessibility;
it does.

The problem lies in the fragmented manner in which these obligations are regulated, and in the absence of any enforcement mechanism strong enough to convert a notified standard into a guaranteed experience.
The structural gaps identified above are not simply the result of poor implementation by cinema owners, streaming platforms, or sports bodies.
They trace back to weaknesses within the RPwD Act itself, which was meant to be the primary legal answer to exactly this problem.
The clearest sign of this weakness came from the judiciary's own reading of the Act.

Union of India, the Supreme Court found that Rule 15 of the RPwD Rules, which used merely "recommendatory" language for accessibility compliance, was ultra vires to the parent Act, and directed the government to frame genuinely mandatory rules instead.

This is significant because it shows that even where Parliament intended accessibility to be a binding obligation, the rules meant to operationalise that obligation were drafted in language weak enough to require judicial correction.

If this is true for accessibility rules in general, the entertainment specific duties under Sections 29 and 30, framed in similarly soft language and never tested this way, are open to the same objection.
A second weakness lies in who the Act actually binds.
Sections 29, 30 and 44 are addressed to government and local authorities, not to private cinema owners, streaming platforms, or event organisers.
Yet most entertainment in India is delivered by private players.

The only reason private entities have begun to bear any accessibility responsibility at all is that courts extended the reasonable accommodation principle laid down by the Hon'ble Court in Vikash Kumar v. UPSC into this space, most notably in Akshat Baldwa v. Yash Raj Films, where a producer was directed to make a film accessible on its OTT release.
This obligation exists today only because one litigant pursued one film.
The Act itself created no general duty on private industry, meaning the entire private sector accessibility regime currently rests on judicial precedent rather than statutory command.

Taken together, these two weaknesses, which are soft rule-making language and a narrow set of duty bearers, explain why the structural deficiencies survive despite a law that appears, prima facie, to address them.
The RPwD Act names accessibility as a right, but leaves its technical content and its private sector reach to be filled in later, by rules not yet framed and litigation not yet filed.

The deficiency existing within India's legal framework summons a comparative examination of jurisdictions that have sought to construe the principles of disability access into concrete requirements for entertainment providers.
The differentiated framework offers possible legislative solutions in addressing the enforcement gap that has been previously identified.
The Americans with Disabilities Act prohibits discrimination on the basis of disability by private entitites operating places of public accommodation, including movie theatres.

More specifically, 28 C.F.R. § 36.303(g) requires covered movie theatres exhibiting digital films distributed with captioning and audio description to provide these accessibility features, subject to applicable exceptions.

The provision also addresses the equipment through which they can access those features, such as the provision of minimum captioning devices or such as the provision of minimum audio description devices and the requirement of notices signifying information about accessible screenings, and mandated staff assistance.

For India, where the accessibility of theatrical releases has continued to generate litigation despite the issuance of standards, examination of such a framework assists us in recognising the value that is carried while actually translating accessibility obligations into specific duties.
The European Model offers a complementary model.
It addresses the regulatory deficiencies within the OTT platforms.

Article 7 of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive, 2010, as amended, requires Member States to ensure that audiovisual media services within their jurisdiction become continuously and progressively more accessible to persons with disabilities through proportionate measures.
It also requires media service providers to report regularly to national regulatory authorities on the implementation of accessibility measures.
Member States must encourage accessibility action plans and designate an accessible, publicly available point of contact for information and complaints concerning accessibility.
Thus, in the present comparative approach, accessibility extends from just being a standard issued, but rather provides a regulatory platform which serves and through which users can raise concerns.
The United Kingdom provides a further comparative point through its Equality Act 2010, with reference to Sections 20 and 29 read with Schedule 2.

Section 29 prohibits discrimination in the provision of services to the public, while Section 20 establishes a duty to make reasonable adjustments where existing arrangements place persons with disabilities at substantial disadvantage.
The interesting part is that the duty in the services is anticipatory.
The service providers are expected to recognise the needs of a person with disability before an individual encounters a barrier and requires an adjustment.
The appropriate adjustment depends upon the circumstances and the reasonableness of the technical accessibility requirements.

For the Indian framework, it raises questions on how the general principles of non-discrimination and reasonable accommodation under the RPwD can be converted into something which is lucid and enforceable.
The deficiencies identified in India's existing framework require more than just some additional accessibility guidelines.
The challenge remains in how the statutory recognition provided under Section 46 of the RPWD Act is translated into clear obligations and into a more potent and operative mechanism of enforcement.
The formative step should be to establish a comprehensive and binding set of accessibility standard which covers different form of entertainment.
The general provisions provided in the RpWd Act shall translate into requirements that entertainment providers can implement and regulators can objectively assess.
The American model can serve as the aspirational framework, which specifies requirements for captioning devices, audio description equipment and staff assistance.

The law must then also clarify the respective responsibilities of the private entertainment industry, and the service providers should be required to consider disability related disadvantages in their own practice.
The accessibility standard then must be accompanied by adequate monitoring and enforcement mechanisms.
The framework should clarify the consequences of non-compliance, which include corrective decisions or, in appropriate cases, proportionate sanctions.
The implementation of such propitious measures must be phased, quantifiable and shall be governed by the experiences of persons with disabilities.
The law must not allow its silence to become the reason a person with disability is denied the joy of entertainment.
A business usually pays GST when it buys goods or services and collects GST when it makes taxable sales.
Subject to the legal conditions, it can use the GST paid on eligible purchases to reduce the GST payable on its sales.
This adjustment is called input tax credit, or ITC.
It helps prevent tax from being charged repeatedly on the same value as goods and services move through the supply chain.
A trader has ₹18,000 of eligible GST credit from purchases and owes ₹27,000 as GST on sales.
If the credit is available for use, the trader can use ₹18,000 of credit and pay the remaining ₹9,000 in cash.
This example leaves aside the separate rules governing different GST components and restrictions on using credit.
The credit is recorded in an online account on the GST portal called the electronic credit ledger.
It is not the same as money in a bank account.
It can be used only in the ways the GST law permits.
If the department blocks the trader's entire ₹18,000 credit in this example, the trader may have to find ₹27,000 in cash to pay the GST due on its sales.
That creates an immediate additional cash requirement of ₹18,000, even before the credit dispute is finally decided.
This is why the right to challenge a block needs a clear timetable.
A business can suffer a serious cash shortage while waiting for a hearing.
The 57th GST Council's recommendation on Rule 86A addresses this problem by proposing an objection mechanism and a personal hearing before the officer decides the objection.
The recommendation itself does not amend the Rules.
It must also be distinguished from a promise of a hearing before every initial block.[1]
Rule 86A allows the Commissioner, or an authorised officer of at least Assistant Commissioner rank, to prevent the use of a specified amount of credit on defined grounds.
The officer must have reasons to believe that the credit was wrongly or fraudulently claimed and must record reasons in writing.
The restriction can affect use of the amount for paying tax or claiming a refund.
It is a temporary protective measure, not a final decision that the taxpayer owes that amount.[2]

The grounds include invoices from suppliers found not to exist, purchases where goods or services were not received, tax charged on invoices that was not paid to the Government, and missing prescribed invoices or documents.
Each ground raises a different question.
Proof that goods arrived may answer an allegation of non-delivery, but may not answer a separate allegation that the supplier failed to pay the tax.
The department has a legitimate reason to act against fake invoices and improper credit claims.
But an officer must connect the restriction to the relevant facts.
CBIC's 2021 guidelines require objective material and caution against mechanical action.
They also provide for reconsideration when the taxpayer produces evidence, including release of part of the restricted credit where justified.[3]
A hearing gives the business a chance to understand the allegation, present its documents and explain why the credit should be released.
The officer must then consider that explanation.
Merely allowing the taxpayer to upload documents is of little help if nobody decides whether the block should continue.
Courts have examined when this opportunity must be given.
In Dee Vee Projects Ltd v Government of Maharashtra, the Bombay High Court recognised that urgent action may be needed but required a hearing after the block.
It indicated that a reasonable period might not extend beyond two weeks.
This is a judicial benchmark from that case, not a two-week deadline written into Rule 86A for every taxpayer across India.[4]
There is also authority supporting a hearing before the initial restriction, except in exceptional circumstances.
In Elitecon International Ltd v Union of India, the Bombay High Court in March 2026 followed the Karnataka appellate approach on this issue.
It also enforced the one-year limit on a block.
The applicable court decisions and the circumstances of the particular case therefore matter.
It would be misleading to say that a prior hearing is always unnecessary.[5]
The taxpayer should be told the legal ground, the invoices or period concerned, the amount blocked and the essential facts supporting the action.
A portal message saying only that credit has been blocked does not explain what the business must prove.
Sensitive investigative information may need protection, but the taxpayer still needs enough detail to give a useful response.
Suppose the allegation is that goods were never delivered.
The business may produce transport records, delivery acknowledgements and stock entries.
If the officer remains unconvinced, the decision should explain why.
If the evidence supports release of only part of the blocked amount, that possibility should be considered.
The review should examine the evidence rather than simply repeat the original allegation.
The proposed procedure should set short periods for communicating the reasons, receiving an objection, holding the hearing and issuing a decision.
Without a decision deadline, an officer could hear the taxpayer and leave the matter pending while the credit remains unusable.
If more time is needed, the officer should explain why and give a revised date.
These are suggestions for designing the procedure.
They should not be presented as deadlines already created by the Council's announcement.
Likewise, automatic release following a missed deadline would need a clear legal basis; it cannot be assumed from the promise of a hearing.
Rule 86A already contains an important outer limit.
Sub-rule (2) allows the restriction to be lifted when the conditions justifying it no longer exist.
Sub-rule (3) makes it cease after one year.
That maximum period does not justify ignoring evidence supporting earlier release.
Equally, expiry of the block does not finally settle whether the underlying credit was lawfully claimed.[6]
The first step is to record the date, amount, officer details and stated reason for the block.
The business should seek the grounds if they have not been communicated.
Its response should connect the disputed invoices to the relevant evidence, rather than simply say that all purchases were genuine.
The request for relief should be specific.

Depending on the facts, the business may seek release of an unsupported amount, reconsideration of particular documents, a hearing, a reasoned decision or recognition that the one-year restriction has expired.
Challenging the temporary block and defending a later demand are separate tasks.
Winning one does not automatically resolve the other.
If the administrative process does not provide relief, the taxpayer should assess the available legal remedy and the relevant court decisions.
Article 226 enables High Court review, while Article 14 protects against arbitrary State action.
A representation to the officer should not be assumed to pause any separately applicable time limit.[7]
The proposed reform will succeed if it produces a decision while the business can still benefit from the relief.
Explaining the allegation, hearing the response and deciding promptly would protect genuine taxpayers while preserving action against improper credit.
A hearing held after months of unexplained delay may satisfy a formality, but it will not restore the cash the business needed when its credit was first blocked.

Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, sections 16 and 49(4); Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017, rule 86A(1); CBIC, Guidelines for disallowing debit of electronic credit ledger under Rule 86A, file CBEC-20/16/05/2021-GST, 2 November 2021, paragraph 3.1.1, reproducing the Rule.

Whether the amended definition of “transgender person” and the removal of statutory recognition of self-perceived gender identity violates Articles 14 , 15 , 19 and 21 and the right to self-identification recognised in NALSA v Union of India (2014)?
On 13 March 2026, the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026 (“Amendment Act”) was tabled in the Lok Sabha.

The Act deleted Section 4(2) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 which stated that “a person recognised as transgender under sub-section (1) shall have a right to self-perceived gender identity.”
It also set up an “authority” consisting of a Chief Medical Officer or a Deputy Chief Medical Officer appointed by the Union government or state government.
It also mandates that transgender persons should be issued a “certificate of identity”.
A transgender person will be entitled to change their first name in the birth certificate or other official documents after the certificate of identity is issued.
Further, the medical institution has to furnish details to the District Magistrate and the authority about the person who underwent surgery.
The Act was passed in the Lok Sabha on 24 March .
It was affirmed in the Rajya Sabha the next day.
It received the President’s assent on 30 March.

During parliamentary debates, opposition members raised concerns regarding the absence of extensive stakeholder consultation, medical board scrutiny, mandatory reporting requirements, the removal of self-identification provisions and the narrowing of legally recognised identities.
Several members sought greater deliberation and referral to a Select Committee.
Amidst protests and an opposition walkout, the Bill was passed by voice vote.

The Union Government defended the legislation as necessary to establish a “precise” and “verifiable” framework for identity recognition, prevent misuse of welfare benefits, and address exploitative practices.
On 24 April 2026, petitioner Laxmi Narayan Tripathi challenged the constitutionality of the Amendment Act under Article 32 of the Constitution.
The petitioner sought that the Amendment Act be declared unconstitutional for violating Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21.
They argued that the Act departs from settled constitutional principles governing dignity, autonomy and gender identity.

The petitioner also challenged the amendment definition of “transgender person” which deletes the statutory recognition of self-perceived identity, amendments introducing certification from a medical authority, and provisions concerning mandatory reporting and penal consequences.
The matter was listed before the Supreme Court on 4 May 2026.

Petitioners argued that the Amendment Act removes the framework of self-recognition and replaces it with medical and bureaucratic verification mechanisms, thereby departing from the principles held in National Legal Services Authority v Union of India (2014) .
In NALSA, the Court recognised transgender persons as rights-bearing constitutional subjects entitled to equality, dignity, autonomy and legal recognition.

It rejected a narrow “biological test” and adopted a “psychological test”, holding that gender identity is fundamentally linked to an individual’s deeply felt sense of self rather than anatomy, chromosomes or surgical status alone.
The Court located self-identification within Articles 14, 19 and 21 and held that constitutional rights cannot be made contingent upon medical procedures or state approval.
The Parliament enacted the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 after the NALSA verdict.

During the May 2026 hearing, the Court considered concerns regarding the shift from self-identification to medical certification, as well as questions relating to possible misuse of identity-based benefits.
The Court also noted objections concerning the maintainability of the challenge since the Amendment Act had not yet been notified.
The Court clarified that it was not going to grant an interim relief at that stage.
It issued notice and placed the matter before a Three-Judge bench.

When The (then) Hon'ble Acting Chief Justice of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court, Justice Gita Mittal paid tribute to Late (Retd.) Justice Leila Seth at the Delhi High Court's Full Court Reference in May 2017 following Justice Seth's demise, she remembered a Judge who was courteous yet firm, composed in court and generous towards young advocates, always giving Counsel's a fair opportunity to be heard.

Justice Seth is rightly remembered as the first woman to be designated a Senior Advocate by the Supreme Court, the first woman judge of the Delhi High Court and the first woman to become Chief Justice of a State High Court in India, but beyond these historic firsts lie two rather unusual stories; bats in a makeshift toilet at The Hon'ble High Court of Judicature at Patna and a grateful litigant who called her “Leila Babu” together both these occurrences offer a glimpse of the woman behind the milestones and the profession she helped change.

Justice Leila Seth was born in Lucknow on the 20 of October, 1930 and studied at Loreto Convent in Darjeeling before moving to England with her husband, where she pursued law while raising a young family.
In 1957, she topped the Bar examinations in England and Wales, becoming the first woman to achieve that distinction.
Such an achievement might have been expected to open doors, but the legal profession had its own ideas about a woman's priorities.
When Justice Seth approached Senior barrister Sachindra Chaudhuri in Calcutta to train under him, he suggested that she marry.
She explained that she was already married.
He then suggested that she have a child, only to learn that she already had one; when he recommended another, she informed him that she already had two.
Chaudhuri eventually relented, telling her, “You're persistent and you will do well at the Bar.”
The exchange is amusing, but its underlying message is less so, despite her qualifications, Justice Seth was made to justify her decision to pursue a career at all.
When she began practising at the Patna High Court in 1959, the profession offered little reassurance that things would be different.
There were only two women advocates there, including Justice Seth, and no proper women's toilet.
Instead, a dusty storeroom had been pressed into service, with one unwelcome feature: bats.
Afraid that one might become entangled in her hair, Justice Seth would cover her head with the end of her sari and hurry out.
When she asked her only female colleague how she managed, the response was blunt, how could Justice Seth expect to practise successfully in Bihar if she was afraid of bats?
It is a wonderfully human anecdote, but it also exposes a basic institutional failure.
Women had entered the profession without even the most elementary provisions being made for their presence.
In another courtroom encounter, when Justice Seth secured the acquittal of a man sentenced to ten years of rigorous imprisonment in a dacoity case.
Grateful for his freedom, he called his advocate “Leila Babu”.
The title was presumably intended as a mark of affection and respect, yet its masculine form carries a quiet irony.
Justice Seth had earned her place through her own legal ability, even as the language of authority remained distinctly male.
She would go on to make that authority her own.
Justice Seth's career at the Bar was marked by the breadth of her practice and the steady accumulation of professional responsibility.

Enrolled at the Calcutta High Court on 16 July 1959 and at the Supreme Court on 7 September that year, she practised in the Patna High Court for nearly a decade, handling tax matters alongside civil, company and criminal cases, matrimonial suits and writ petitions.
From 1963 to 1968, she served as Junior Standing Counsel for the Income-tax Department in Bihar and was also on the panel of lawyers representing the State of Bihar before the Patna High Court.
In 1972, she began practising in the Delhi High Court and the Supreme Court, taking on a wide range of civil, tax, constitutional and other matters.
On 10 January 1977, she was designated a Senior Advocate by the Supreme Court, another milestone in a career built through years of demanding legal work.
One of her most memorable cases involved a railway engine driver and a guard prosecuted after people travelling on the roof of their train were killed when it passed beneath a low bridge.
The driver faced imprisonment and the possible loss of his livelihood, yet could afford barely a day's legal fees.

Justice Seth took up his defence and examined the technical questions at the heart of the case, including whether he could have heard the people on the roof and whether the train could have been stopped in time.
The driver later returned with his family and presented her with a tin of homemade ghee.

What stayed with her for years was a small gift from a man who had very little to offer, a simple gesture through which he expressed his gratitude to a lawyer who had made a genuine difference to his life.

It was not the value of the gift that made it memorable, but what it represented, the trust he had placed in someone whose work had helped protect not just his livelihood, but the future he was trying to build.
On 25 July 1978, Justice Seth was appointed an Additional Judge of the Delhi High Court and became a permanent judge on 18 July 1980.
On 5 August 1991, she became Chief Justice of the Himachal Pradesh High Court, the first woman to head a State High Court in India.
Her career had taken her from a profession that questioned whether she belonged in it to the highest judicial office she could hold in a State High Court.
The significance lay not simply in reaching these positions, but in demonstrating that women could occupy them on the strength of their own ability.
Justice Seth's commitment to justice continued beyond the Bench.
As a member of the Fifteenth Law Commission of India from 1997 to 2000, she contributed to efforts to reform women's property rights.
The wider reform process culminated in the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, which strengthened daughters' rights in Mitakshara coparcenary property.
The change mattered for more than inheritance, property could mean financial security, greater independence and the freedom to make choices on one's own terms.
In 2012, Justice Seth also served on the Justice J. Verma Committee, constituted after the Delhi gang rape to recommend reforms to the law on sexual violence.
Its report informed significant criminal law reforms in 2013, although not all its recommendations were adopted.
She also opposed the criminalisation of consensual same-sex relations following the Supreme Court's decision in Suresh Kumar Koushal v.
Across these causes, she continued to challenge legal and social assumptions that restricted people's rights.
Her writing brought these concerns to readers beyond the legal profession.

In her autobiography, On Balance, she reflected on the experiences that shaped her life and career, while her book We, the Children of India introduced young readers to the Constitution and its Preamble.

In another of her books, Talking of Justice: People's Rights in Modern India, she explored questions of rights and equality, extending her engagement with the law beyond the courtroom and into public life.

Through these books, Justice Leila Seth conveyed a conviction that ran throughout her career, that the law should not remain the preserve of those trained to practise it, but should be understood by the people whose lives it governs.
Justice Leila Seth died on 5 May 2017, aged 86, having lived a life that changed the Indian legal profession in ways both visible and lasting.
Her journey from a young advocate navigating a profession that was barely prepared for women to becoming the first woman Chief Justice of a State High Court is remarkable in itself.
But it is the smaller stories, too, that make her memorable: the bats that frightened her in Patna and the grateful litigant who called her “Leila Babu”.
Justice Seth never allowed the attitudes of her time to decide how far she could go.
She built her career on her own terms and continued to speak and work for equality long after leaving the Bench.
She once described the world she wished for as one in which people could “walk hand in hand, not a step in front or a step behind”.
That simple thought seems an apt way to remember her, not only for what she achieved, but for the fairness and dignity she believed everyone deserved.
Perhaps that is what makes her story endure.
She entered a profession that had not quite made room for her, and left it a little more open for those who came after.
The bats and the Babu may be the stories we remember with a smile, but Justice Leila Seth's true legacy is the path she helped clear for others.
On 7 August 2023, The Digital Data Protection (DPDP) Bill was passed in the Lok Sabha.
Subsequently, the Bill was passed in the Rajya Sabha and received the President’s assent.
The Bill was enacted on 11 August 2023.
The Act brought about several provisions to regulate and penalise unauthorised use of personal data by companies and big firms.

On 2 February 2026, Venkatesh Nayak, an RTI activist filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution, challenging Sections 17(1)(c), 17(2), 33(1), 36 and 44(3) of the DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 17 and 23(2) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (DPDP Rules).
The petition argues that the provisions violate Article 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution.
Two other petitions—by Nitin Sethi and The Reporters Collective–were filed subsequently.
Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act amended Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 which exempts the disclosure of any information “which relates to personal information”.
The petitioners claim that this amendment creates a “blanket ban on the obligation to disclose personal information”.
This will allow the executive to deny information to citizens by citing the “personal nature of the information”.
Petitioners argue that this will violate the right to information and the right to know, which is traced to Article 19(1)(a)—the fundamental right to speech and expression.

Previously, the Supreme Court in CPIO, Supreme Court v Subhash Aggarwal (2019) had held that there is no bar under the RTI Act on disclosure of personal information, given that the information does not cause invasion of privacy and has a reasonable nexus with public activity and public interest.

Petitioners have also challenged Section 17(1)(c), which allows the processing of data in the “interest of prevention, detection, investigation or prosecution of any offence or contravention of any law for the time being in force in India”.

Section 17(2) states that the Act will not be applicable when data is processed by the Union government, or any authority it may notify, in the “interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, maintenance of public order or preventing incitement to any cognizable offence relating to any of these”.
The petitioners are apprehensive that the provisions will result in a “surveillance regime”, with no safeguards or review mechanism.
This, according to them, is manifestly arbitrary and violates Article 14.
Section 36 of the law also states that any intermediary or data fiduciary should furnish information which is required by the Union government.
This, the petitioners claim, allows the Union to call information without any “statutory guidance”.

Further, Rule 23(2) compels the fiduciary or intermediary to not disclose to the data principal that such information was furnished to the Union government if it is likely to “affect the sovereignty and integrity of India or security of the State”.
Section 18 of the DPDP Act calls for the establishment of a Data Protection Board of India.
Rules 17(1) and 17(2) of the DPDP Rules provide for a search cum selection committee for the appointment of the Chairperson and other members of the Board.
Petitioners claim that the “executive dominance” in the formation of the Committee violates the doctrine of the separation of powers.
Lastly, Section 33(1) imposes penalties for “significant” data breaches.
The petitioners claim that the wording of the provision is vague as there is no statutory guidance to determine what constitutes a “significant” breach.
On 16 February 2026, the Bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V.M. Pancholi heard the matter and issued notice to parties.
The Bench refused to grant an interim stay on the DPDP Act.
Further, the Court referred the matter to a larger bench to be heard in March 2026.
Around the October protest at Jantar Mantar, the Delhi Police took a large number of people into custody.
Police sources put the figure on the day itself at over 7,000.
A handful of organisers were placed under “preventive arrest” and produced before a Special Executive Magistrate.
These labels are not interchangeable, and the choice between them is not a technicality.
It decides whether the constitutional safeguards against arbitrary arrest apply at all.

One person detained during the protests, who asked not to be named, told me that they were picked up by the police near Mandi House and later left at Narela, on the northern edge of the city, roughly 40 kilometres away.
Whatever its legal label, that is a period of custody, and it raises the question this article addresses:
which safeguards apply to it?
Reports so far point to at least three legal routes.
The president of a student organisation was detained under Section 65 of the Delhi Police Act, 1978 and released.
One of the organisers was arrested under Sections 126 and 170 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and produced before a Special Executive Magistrate.
And a petition now before the Supreme Court challenges the use of Section 172 of the BNSS against those detained or turned back on their way to the protest.

Section 65 of the Delhi Police Act obliges every person to conform to the reasonable directions of a police officer and lets the officer restrain or remove anyone who does not, either taking the person before a magistrate or, in trivial cases, releasing them once the occasion has passed.
Section 172 of the BNSS, which has no equivalent in the 1973 Code, now does much the same thing for the whole country.

Every person must conform to the “lawful directions” of a police officer given under the preventive chapter, and the officer “may detain or remove any person resisting, refusing, ignoring or disregarding” such a direction, before either taking the person to a Magistrate or, “in petty cases”, releasing them within twenty-four hours.
Neither provision uses the word “arrest”.
Neither requires the officer to record reasons.
Neither says what makes a direction reasonable or lawful, or what counts as a “petty” case.
Section 170, by contrast, is an arrest power:
it permits arrest without warrant of a person “designing to commit” a cognizable offence.
It at least engages Chapter V of the BNSS and the duty to produce the arrested person before a Magistrate.
Article 22(1) requires that a person who is arrested be informed of the grounds of arrest as soon as may be.
Article 22(2) requires production before the nearest magistrate within twenty-four hours.
State(NCT of Delhi), 2024 INSC 414, the Supreme Court held that the grounds must be communicated, and that a failure to do so vitiates the arrest and the remand that follows.

State of Haryana, 2025 INSC 162, it added that the burden of proving compliance lies on the police, that telling a relative or preparing an arrest memo does not suffice, and that once a violation is shown, the court must order release.
These are among the strongest liberty protections the Court has developed in recent years.

The petition challenging Section 172 makes this point directly that by using “detain or remove" rather than “arrest”, the provision allows the police to restrain a person without triggering the safeguards of Chapter V or Article 22(1), (2) and (5).
The same is true of Section 65 of the Delhi Police Act.
A person held in a bus or a police station for several hours is in custody in every practical sense, whether or not the police record it as an arrest.
On the present structure of the law, that person may have no grounds to be told and no magistrate to be produced before.
The question the courts must now answer is whether Article 22 turns on the label the police choose or on the fact of custody.
There is a strong case for the second answer.
Article 22 protects against the deprivation of liberty by the executive without judicial oversight.

A reading that allows the executive to escape that protection by calling an arrest a “detention” would hollow out Purkayastha and Vihaan Kumar in exactly the situations, large-scale preventive detentions, where they are most likely to be needed.
The police's position deserves to be set out fully.
In the contempt proceedings arising from the restrictions, the Delhi Police Commissioner has told the Supreme Court that no one was illegally detained.
The police say permission for the protest was refused because notice was given late, and a prohibitory order under Section 163 of the BNSS was in force.
On the NSA, the Delhi Police have said that the delegation of detention power under Section 3(2) is a routine quarterly renewal that predates the protests.
And in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court itself accepted that protest at Jantar Mantar may be regulated.
These points go to whether the restrictions were justified.
They do not answer the Article 22 question.
MKSS permits regulation of a protest site.
It does not authorise the interception of individuals at airports and railway stations, far from the site, before any direction could have been given to them at all.
A prohibitory order under Section 163 may make an assembly unlawful, but it does not by itself supply the individual grounds that Article 22(1) requires for each person deprived of liberty.
And if, as the police say, the detentions were lawful, it should be straightforward to show what direction each detainee disregarded, when, and why it was lawful.
Vihaan Kumar places that burden on the police.
Section 172 matters most because it is national.
What was once a Delhi-specific police-act power is now available to every police force in India, in a form that the arrest safeguards may not reach.

If it becomes a routine tool of crowd management, the protections of Purkayastha and Vihaan Kumar will protect the person who is formally arrested, but not the larger number who are held without being arrested.

First, the Supreme Court should hold, in the pending challenge or otherwise, that the safeguards of Article 22(1) and (2), as explained in Purkayastha and Vihaan Kumar, apply to any custodial restraint under Section 172 of the BNSS or Section 65 of the Delhi Police Act, whatever the police choose to call it.
Grounds should be given at the time of detention, preferably in writing, and a record should be kept of each detention, its duration and the direction disregarded.

Second, Section 172 should be read down, or amended by Parliament, so that a “lawful direction” is one that is necessary to prevent a specific cognizable offence and proportionate to that risk, and so that "petty cases" are defined.
Without these limits, the provision is capable of operating as a general power of detention without the safeguards that accompany arrest.
Third, where organisers are proceeded against under Sections 126 and 170, the security proceedings should be decided by a Judicial Magistrate rather than an Executive Magistrate.
The authority that decides whether a person may be bound over to keep the peace should be independent of the executive that initiated the proceedings.
None of this prevents the police from maintaining order.
It requires only that when the State takes a person into custody, it says why, keeps a record, and answers to a court.
Those obligations should not depend on the word the police choose to write in the register.
On 24 June, the Election Commission of India (ECI) announced that it will begin a Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls in Bihar ahead of its state assembly elections.
The exercise aims to revise the electoral rolls in the state in order to include all eligible voters and eliminate all ineligible voters from the voter list.
The notification said that the ECI would “scrupulously” adhere to the Constitutional provisions regarding eligibility and disqualification of voters in the revision of the electoral roll.
This, the ECI said, was clearly laid down under Article 326 of the Constitution of India and Section 16 of the Representation of People Act, 1950 (RPA).
Article 326 states that any person above the age of 18 is eligible to vote.
Section 16 sets down the criteria for a person who is disqualified from being a voter.
These criteria include not being a citizen of India, being of unsound mind, or being disqualified from voting under any law related to corrupt practices and other election offenses.
The notification stated that the SIR is carried out through its powers under Article 324 and Section 21 of the RPA.
Article 324 vests the ECI with superintendence, direction and control over elections in India.
Section 21 of the RPA empowers the ECI to prepare and revise electoral rolls.
The qualifying date for the SIR was set at 1 July 2025.
Therefore, any person who turned 18 on or before that date would be eligible.

According to the notification, this is the first intensive revision of the Bihar rolls since 2003 and aims to maintain “the integrity of the Electoral Roll” as it is “fundamental for the conduct of free & fair elections”.
It aims to achieve three things in Bihar:

The ECI has justified this intensified exercise, citing factors such as rapid urbanisation, frequent migration, the addition of newly eligible young voters, underreporting of deaths and the inclusion of names of foreign illegal immigrants.
The ECI has delegated Booth Level Officers (BLOs) to conduct house-to-house verification.
This will include door-to-door surveys by the BLOs who will identify eligible or non-eligible voters.
It has designated Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) to print pre-filled Enumeration Forms for existing electors.
The BLOs will distribute the enumeration forms and collect them with supporting documents during their visits.
These forms will be available to download on the ECI website (or ECINET).
Alternatively, electors can fill out and upload these forms online along with relevant documents.
To enhance transparency while maintaining voter privacy, the notification stated that the documents used for verifying eligibility will be uploaded on ECINET.
They will be accessible only to authorised election officials.
The ECI has invited active participation from all political parties and has urged them to appoint Booth Level Agents (BLAs) for every polling booth.
This way “discrepancies, if any, are resolved at the preparation stage itself, thereby reducing the instances of filing claims, objections and appeals.”
The claims and objections can be filed by any elector or political party.
These complaints will be assessed by the Assistant Electoral Registration Officers (AEROs).
The final electoral roll will be published by the ERO after all claims and objections have been addressed.
This roll will be shared with recognised political parties and made publicly accessible on the websites of the ECI and the Chief Electoral Officer.
The draft electoral rolls will go live on 1 August 2025 .
In early July, the Association for Democratic Reforms, Swaraj Party member and activist Yogendra Yadav, moved the Supreme Court under Article 32 , challenging the ECI’s notification.
They claim that the SIR is arbitrary and violative of the universal right to adult suffrage.
The petitions argue that the exercise excludes indicators like Aadhaar and ration cards and makes the proof of parents’ identity mandatory.
Given Bihar’s high rates of poverty and migration, such requirements may disenfranchise millions.

The petitions also criticise the short timeframe and absence of prior consultation, arguing that the exercise undermines democracy, equality, and the right to vote, particularly for the most vulnerable.
Further, they point out that for the exercise to be fulfilled within the timeline, the ECI will need to train one lakh BLOs, of which 20,000 are yet to be employed.
“All within the month (of which a week has passed) when Bihar is in the midst of the monsoon and floods!

So, unless the ECI has a magic wand, we should expect a withdrawal of this order, drastic changes in the list of documents allowed (as announced on June 30) or a postponement of the Bihar assembly elections,” the ADR exclaimed in its petition.
The petitions pray for an immediate stay on the SIR.
In the meantime, the ECI has published notices of the smooth implementation of the SIR in the State on 4 and 5 July on its official website.
On 6 July, the ECI issued a press release stating that the initial phase of the SIR has been completed.
Notably, the release clarifies that there has been no change in the process of the SIR and will continue as per the notification released on 24 June.
Moreover, it carries the phrase: “No changes made in SIR as being rumoured by some”.
On 4 February, the Court issued notice in a petition by Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee challenging SIR in West Bengal.
SIR had begun in the state on 4 November 2025.
On 27 May 2026, the Supreme Court unanimously upheld the Bihar SIR exercise.
The Bench ruled that adopting a different procedure from routine electoral roll revisions does not make the exercise unconstitutional.
It stated that measures adopted in the SIR are not manifestly excessive or disproportionate.
The SIR secures the mandate of free and fair elections.
While presumption of validity exists when included in an electoral roll, that presumption can be rebutted.

On 19 October 2026, we wrote in ThePrint about the Supreme Court’s recent judgment in Yes Bank Limited v Axis Trustee Services Limited 2026 INSC 1132 setting aside the write-down of Yes Bank’s Additional Tier 1 (AT-1) bonds.
We argued that the judgment is legally sound and underscores, once again, significant gaps in India’s framework for resolving distressed financial institutions.
The judgment also brings us back to two posts we published on this Blog in 2023, when the litigation was at an earlier stage.

In our first post , we had welcomed the Bombay High Court’s decision similarly setting aside the write-down, but we also criticised its reluctance to examine the fairness of writing down AT-1 bonds while sparing equity shareholders.
We argued that the doctrine of legitimate expectations provided an additional basis for scrutinising the administrator’s decision.
In our second post , we considered the implications of the Credit Suisse rescue, in which Swiss authorities similarly wrote down AT-1 bonds while preserving some value for shareholders.

We noted that banking authorities in the United Kingdom and European Union had publicly reaffirmed the conventional creditor hierarchy, and wondered whether these developments might influence the Indian Supreme Court’s approach.
In this post, we examine the Court’s reasoning more closely than was possible in our newspaper column.
It is tempting to view the Supreme Court’s judgment as one largely based on technical and procedural grounds.
In fact, the Court’s decision is consequential for regulatory governance, particularly the governance of distressed financial institutions in India.
The doctrine of legitimate expectations, as we argued earlier, remains important in defining the limits of regulatory discretion when dealing with distressed financial firms.
The dispute arose from Yes Bank’s reconstruction in March 2020.
Following the imposition of a moratorium, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) superseded the bank’s board and appointed an administrator under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
The Central Government notified a reconstruction scheme on 13 March 2020.
The following day, the RBI-appointed administrator ordered the complete write-down of two tranches of AT-1 bonds aggregating ₹8,415 crore.
That is, the value of the AT-1 bonds was driven down to zero, while the equity shares were left intact.
The AT-1 bondholders challenged this write-down before the Bombay High Court, which ruled in their favour in January 2023.
Yes Bank and the RBI appealed to the Supreme Court.
Nearly four years, twenty three hearings and six bench changes later, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeals on 15 October 2026.

The Supreme Court’s reasoning rests on three closely connected questions: what the reconstruction scheme authorised, who possessed the power to write down the bonds, and when that power could lawfully be exercised.
A major part of its ruling is underpinned by legitimate expectations.

To discern the import of this omission, the Supreme Court scrutinised the representations submitted by the bond trustees, regulatory proposals from the RBI, and inter-departmental correspondence between the RBI and the Department of Financial Services.
This record revealed that the bondholders had actively protested the total write-down, offering instead to convert their bonds into equity shares of Yes Bank.
Evaluating the deletion in this backdrop, the Supreme Court held that the proposition to write down or convert the bonds had been consciously abandoned by the Central Government.
It set aside the Administrator’s decision on this basis:

For the Administrator to then turn volte-face the decision of the Central Government by writing down the AT-1 Bonds entirely, did away with the deliberative process that occurred between the Draft Scheme and the Reconstruction Scheme….[I]t would be unreasonable to infer that the RBI and the Central Government would undertake the entirety of a long-drawn process of crafting the Reconstruction Scheme and seemingly leave out the crucial part concerning the AT-1 Bonds.”
The significance of this finding extends beyond the Yes Bank restructuring.
Where the state follows a formal process of consultation, deliberation and notification, the resulting instrument must mean something.

This is a profound departure from the earlier deferential approach generally adopted by the judiciary towards regulatory consultations, which are often held to have no ‘binding effect’ on the final notification of regulations or regulatory actions.

Next, the RBI and Yes Bank contended that even in the absence of specific provisions, the general residuary provisions of the reconstruction scheme empowered the administrator to effectuate a write-down of the AT-1 bonds.
The Supreme Court rejected this reliance on residuary authority.

While it is true that the Administrator’s residuary powers are preserved under the aforementioned clause, such a general savings provision does not, by itself, confer the specific authority to write down the AT-1 Bonds after YES BANK came to be reconstructed…[I]t is a settled legal principle that a power not specifically conferred cannot be implicitly vested through a general, omnibus savings clause.
To that extent, we rule against YES BANK and the Administrator.”
This part of the ruling is most significant as general residuary powers are ubiquitous in every law conferring powers on the regulators or executive agencies.
The Court’s ruling on this specific issue implies that these omnibus residuary provisions do not empower regulators to alter or extinguish contractual rights.
Such powers, if at all, must be specifically hard-coded in the law or the executive notification.
The above parts of the Supreme Court’s judgment speak to the doctrine of legitimate expectations, even while the Court does not specifically refer to this doctrine nor was it pleaded by the parties.

The legitimate expectations doctrine is an administrative law principle that holds public authorities accountable when they repudiate a clear promise, representation, or deviate from established practice without reason.
The doctrine does not go as far as creating a legal right or guaranteeing a specific outcome to persons whose expectations have been violated by the state.
However, it does create space for contestation of state actions that violate ‘legitimate expectations’ set by established practice, past representations or good faith.

Indian courts have applied this doctrine to set aside executive actions of various kinds, such as a government notification that suddenly excluded some areas from a slum clearance scheme, and the suspension of a previously issued license for setting up a school.
It recently applied this doctrine to enforce the Jharkhand Government’s promise to grant a 50% exemption from electricity duty for five years to power plants.
The core judicial concern was not the mere reality of investor loss.
AT-1 instruments are inherently speculative debt, and investors cannot claim protection against risks bargain-for under their terms.

The true constitutional defect was that the state, through its administrator, imposed targeted losses upon one tier of capital while safeguarding another, failing to offer a rational basis for disturbing the conventional hierarchy of loss absorption.
In evaluating this departure, the doctrine of legitimate expectations offers a vital evaluative standard.
The Court’s judgment speaks to this doctrine, although not in the context we had argued.

The Court observed that after the consultations between the bondholders and the RBI during the intervening period between the draft reconstruction scheme and the final scheme, the government eventually dropped the AT-1 write-down provisions from the final scheme:

“ 40. …[W]e have good reasons to infer that the Central Government had taken a conscious decision to exclude the clause permitting writing down of the AT-1 Bonds from the Reconstruction Scheme, based on consideration of the objections lodged.

If it were the intention of the Central Government to allow the Administrator to write down the AT-1 Bonds after publication of the Reconstruction Scheme even after exclusion of the relevant clause from the Draft Scheme, that would have made it susceptible to face the criticism of acting clandestinely and the accusation of committing an act amounting to a fraud on public.”
Effectively, the Court found that the dropping of the write-down provisions from the final scheme created a legitimate expectation that the bonds will not be written down by the Administrator.

In our view, therefore, the judgment creates scope – perhaps, for the first time in the history of resolving distressed financial institutions in India – to circumscribe regulatory powers with this doctrine.
Where regulators invoke broad residual powers, the doctrine of legitimate expectations supplies a critical yardstick of reasonableness and fairness.
Promulgated practices and market expectations cannot be arbitrarily discarded;
they constrain the exercise of residual executive power even during stressful times such as financial resolution.
Finally, as we have argued earlier, the Yes Bank judgment exposes a deeper deficiency in India’s framework for resolving financial institutions.
Banks cannot be resolved under the ordinary insolvency regime applicable to non-financial enterprises:
their failure implicates depositors, payment systems, systemic stability and the risk of contagion.
A specialised resolution regime is therefore indispensable.

India’s capacity for bank-specific interventions is no substitute for a coherent statutory framework governing the initiation of resolution, the allocation of powers, the hierarchy of claims and procedural safeguards for affected creditors and investors.
The Financial Resolution and Deposit Insurance Bill, introduced in 2017 and subsequently withdrawn, was an earlier attempt to address this lacuna.
Its political fate does not diminish the legislative imperative.

The challenge is to reconcile regulatory discretion with legal certainty: preserving the capacity for decisive intervention in a crisis while ensuring that its consequences remain reasonably foreseeable.
This is not merely a question of investor protection.
Where the treatment of claims in resolution is uncertain, investors demand a premium for regulatory risk, ultimately raising banks’ cost of capital and, with it, the cost of financial intermediation.
The Supreme Court’s Yes Bank judgment should not be read as repudiating the loss-absorbing function of AT-1 bonds.
What the Court rejected was the exercise of write-down powers by an authority lacking lawful competence, at a time inconsistent with the prescribed framework.
The Court’s judgment finally settles a principle long ignored in matters of financial regulatory governance:
The resolution of financial distress demands decisive intervention, not exemption from the rule of law.
Filed as a Public Interest Litigation, the petition challenges what it describes as the “subversion of multi-member decision making” within the Election Commission of India (ECI).
It concerns decisions and software modifications allegedly undertaken in the ECI’s name without concurrence of the other two Election Commissioners: Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.

The challenge follows an Indian Express report which recorded at least 14 formal objections made by Sandhu and Joshi over decisions concerning electoral rolls, Form 6 and the centralisation of electoral-roll management.
The objections included concerns over access to the ECI’s ECINet and ERONet systems.

The petition relies on Article 324 of the Constitution, which vests the superintendence, direction and control of electoral rolls in the ECI, and Article 326 , which provides for elections on the basis of adult suffrage.
It invokes Articles 14 , 19(1)(a) and 21 in relation to equality, political expression and civic dignity.
Additionally, the petition refers to Article 361 to argue that the CEC does not enjoy personal immunity from criminal proceedings.
At the centre of the petition is Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023.
It says that the ECI may unanimously regulate the procedure for transacting and allocating its business among members.
It further provides that ECI business should, as far as possible, be transacted unanimously and that differences between the Commissioners are to be decided by majority.
Seshan v Union of India (1995) to argue that the CEC is primus inter pares , or first among equals.
The next challenge concerns Form 6, the statutory form for voter registration.
Petitioners submit that a question was added in July 2026 requiring applicants to provide details of their inclusion in the electoral roll after the last SIR.
Joshi earlier recorded that Form 6 could not be changed without a formal amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, a position with which Sandhu concurred.
The petition alleges that the digital modification was made without such an amendment and seeks restoration of the statutory form.

Regarding centralisation of the electoral-roll database through ECINet, the petition relies on Section 13B of the RPA, which provides for Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) to prepare and revise electoral rolls.
Joshi and Sandhu reported that a number of EROs are unable to access the database.
Joshi objected to the “gradual centralisation” that occurs as a consequence, while Sandhu recorded that the Director General (IT) had “no legal authority” to restrict access of statutory authorities.
Another challenge concerns 97 electors in Goa.
The petition states that after electors were found eligible by the local EROs, the ECINet system did not have a “rollback/reversal” facility to restore their entries.
It refers to eight communications sent by the Goa Chief Electoral Officer in February 2026 seeking activation of the facility and alleges that the electors were ultimately left out of the final roll.
16.10 lakh appeals filed before Appellate Tribunals in West Bengal have also been challenged.
These appeals were filed in ECI’s name against electors whose inclusion followed verification by Judicial Officers.
The petition relies on Sandhu’s objection to unilateral authorisation of the appeals.
Invoking Section 32 of the RPA, the petition highlights criminal liability of officials for certain breaches of duty.

It also refers to Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article 25 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights in support of its claims concerning participation in public life and elections.
On 29 September 2026, a Bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana agreed to list the petition next week after Senior Advocate Vikas Singh sought an early hearing.
Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd. challenged an arbitral award in December 2021 and learned which court could hear the challenge only in September 2026.
A challenge in the wrong court can lose years to a jurisdictional objection.
Two decisions of the Supreme Court this year, J&K Economic Reconstruction Agency v. Ltd. , were expected to settle where that petition belongs.

This post argues that, read together, they settle the position where the parties have named a seat, but adopt two different methods where they have not named a seat, without acknowledging the difference.
It argues that Mahanadi should be confined to its unusual facts.

In Rash Builders , decided under the Jammu and Kashmir Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1997 (“J&K Act”), a statute modelled on the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the parties agreed before the tribunal that Srinagar would be the seat and New Delhi the venue.
Hearings were held, and the award was signed in New Delhi, which was recorded in the award as the place of arbitration.
Consequently, the Jammu and Kashmir High Court returned the petition seeking to set aside the arbitral award under section 34 for want of jurisdiction.

However, the Supreme Court reversed it, holding that the seat is fixed by the parties’ agreement, not by a “stray recital” in the award, and that it remains fixed unless the parties expressly agree otherwise.
The result is correct, but one provision goes unmentioned.
Section 31(4) of the Act, like its J&K counterpart, requires the award to state the place of arbitration “as determined in accordance with Section 20” and deems the award to have been made there.
What the Court called a recital is thus a statutory requirement.
A place that departs from the agreed seat is not one so determined, so the deeming fiction never attaches.
Yet the Court’s silence leaves open whether such a misstatement is simply to be ignored, or is itself a defect that may be raised in a challenge.

Rash Builders also restated the two tests for a seat the parties have not named: the “closest and most intimate connection” test from Naviera Amazonica , and the Shashoua principle , under which a designated venue may be read as the seat where the agreement and circumstances so indicate.
Mahanadi presented that situation in its starkest form.
The contract had no arbitration clause and the Orissa High Court, with the parties’ consent, appointed a sole arbitrator under section 11(6) without naming a seat or venue.
The proceedings took place in Cuttack, and the High Court later treated Cuttack as the seat.

The Supreme Court held that neither the place of hearings nor the location of the appointing court makes a seat, a proposition consistent with State of West Bengal v. Associated Contractors and Hindustan Construction Co.
However, the Court did not identify the seat.
It neither applied the closest connection test nor the Shashoua principle, and did not even cite Rash Builders .

Instead, it turned to the definition of “Court” in section 2(1)(e), read with section 42, and held that, absent an agreement or a direction in the appointment order, any commercial or district court within the High Court’s territorial jurisdiction (based on where the cause of action arose) could entertain the section 34 petition.
The two decisions thus rest on different premises.
For Rash Builders , a missing seat is a gap to be filled by the parties’ intention;
for Mahanadi , it vests jurisdiction in the ordinary rules governing civil courts.
Both are decisions of benches of equal strength, and neither engages the other.
A court facing an agreement silent on the seat has no clear guidance on which to follow.

It may be said that Mahanadi simply returns the position of law to BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC Ltd. , which recognised that, where no seat is designated, the courts identified by section 2(1)(e) on cause-of-action principles retain jurisdiction, and that a case with no arbitration clause offered little intention to ascertain.
The second point is the stronger, and may well justify the result on these facts.
It does not explain why the tests restated in Rash Builders months earlier were bypassed without discussion, or which approach governs the more common case of a written clause that names no seat.

For contract drafters, the lesson is to use the word “seat”, name a place, and make any exclusive jurisdiction clause expressly subject to the arbitration agreement, given the High Courts’ readiness to treat such clauses as seat designations.
“Venue” should never be left to do the work of a seat.
Where a clause is silent, parties to a section 11 application should ask the appointing court to specify the seat, a direction Mahanadi treats as decisive.
Mahanadi shows the cost of not doing so.
Petitions filed in 2021 spent nearly five years on a jurisdictional objection before a word was said on the merits.
Tribunals fixing the seat in a first procedural order should record the parties’ express consent.
Both the above-mentioned 2026 decisions give full effect to party autonomy where it has been exercised.
However, where it has not, the Court has moved from ascertaining intention to applying default jurisdictional rules, without acknowledging the shift or reconciling the two approaches.
Consequently, the method for determining a seat the parties never named is unclear.
Mahanadi is best confined to its unusual facts: a reference made without any arbitration clause, with no intention to find.
Where a written clause merely omits the seat, the tests restated in Rash Builders should continue to govern, with section 2(1)(e) as the last resort rather than the first.
Until a larger bench or Parliament resolves that question, precise drafting remains the only reliable safeguard.

The petitioner, Ghazi Saaduddin is a resident of Aurangabad, Maharashtra who contested the Municipal Corporation election from Ward No. 68—a seat reserved for candidates from the Scheduled Caste category.
He claimed to belong to the “Madari” caste, which is listed as Scheduled Caste at Entry 46 under Part X of the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950 .
He was declared elected on 13 April 2000.

On 26 April, the defeated candidate, Mr Chandne filed a complaint with the Municipal Commissioner, seeking to disqualify Saaduddin on the grounds that a person professing Islam cannot claim SC status.
On the advice of the State Election Commission, the matter was referred to the Schedule Caste Verification Committee.
By order dated 28 August 2000, the Committee invalidated Saaduddin’s claim.
Challenging the said order, he filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the Bombay High Court.

The petition further challenged a Government Resolution (GR) dated 21 March 1979, which amended Clause 3 of the Constitution SC Order, 1950 to declare that “no person who professes a religion different from the Hindu or the Sikh or Buddhist religion shall be deemed to be a member of a Scheduled Caste.”

A similar matter came up before the Court in Soosai v Union of India (1995), where the petitioner—a Hindu from an Adi-Dravidian caste—claimed that he was deprived of SC welfare assistance due to his conversion to Christianity.
The Court dismissed his plea, citing Clause 3 of SC Order, 1950.
It noted the lack of sufficient evidence “to show that the same caste continues after conversion.”
Multiple petitions on the question of SC status post religious conversion were tagged with Saaduddin’s petition.
One of these is a 2004 petition filed by the Centre for Public Interest Litigation.
On 29 October 2004, the Government of India constituted the National Commission for Religious and Linguistic Minorities, headed by former Chief Justice of India, Ranganathan Mishra .
The Committee submitted its report in 2007 and recommended extending the benefit of SC reservations to Dalits who have converted to Christianity and Islam.
While the Supreme Court considered the findings of the Committee, the central government discarded the same, deeming the report “flawed”.
Subsequently, in 2022, it constituted another committee, under the Section 3 of the Commission of Inquiry Act, 1952 , to be led by former CJI, K.
The committee is yet to submit a report.

On 30 April 2025, Advocate Ashwini Kumar Upadhyay filed a public interest litigation, seeking directions to the Centre to establish a Legal Education Commission or an Expert Committee to review the syllabus, curriculum and duration of Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees in Law.
The petition contends that an updated framework is urgently required to mark a break from the current 5-year curriculum, which is “exorbitant” and “disincentivizing” for law students.
In 1986, Professor Jill Cottrell, Senior Lecturer in Law in the University of Warwick published a paper in the Journal of Legal Education, tracing the foundations of Legal Education in India.

He noted that legal education in India has always been a graduate subject—a student shall hold a Bachelor’s in Arts, Commerce or Science before embarking on the study of law, after which a three-year degree course (called the LL.B. or B.L.) may be undertaken.
Therefore, 10 + 2 + 3 + 3 was the common design for obtaining a law degree.

As early as 1983, the Bar Council of India (BCI) introduced the 5-Year LL.B. programme, offering an alternative curriculum design of 10 + 2 + 5, which enabled students to study law immediately after completing their secondary education.
With its establishment the National Law School University of India (NLSIU), it became one of the first universities to adopt the integrated programme.
The 3-Year LL.B. program still continues today for those who take up law after completing any other degree.
There are 27 National Law Schools offering five-year courses such as B.A.
Admission to these courses are carried out through the Common Law Entrance Test or CLAT.
Private universities take admissions either through CLAT or their own entrance examinations.

Upadhyay’s petition notes that while the Ministry of Education has promoted 4-year Bachelor’s Degrees across professional and educational courses through the New Education Policy (NEP) 2020 , the Bar Council of India (BCI) has failed to implement the same in law degrees.
It claims that the current 5-year duration deprives law students of opportunities available under the NEP, making the program needlessly long and financially burdensome.
The petition additionally suggests that humanities or commerce subjects should be dropped from the Bachelor’s curriculum since they stretch the duration of the program.
It notes that revising the duration of LL.B. programs to four years will allow students to pursue academic opportunities, prepare for competitive exams or gain work experience sooner.
The petition suggests that students may look for internships, job opportunities or prepare for competitive exams in the 5th year after their 4-year degree.
It also recommends replacing the 5-year BA/BBA-LL.B. with an integrated LL.B.-LL.M..
Similar petitions challenging the BCI Rules regarding LL.M. programs are already before the Supreme Court.
In January 2021, the Bar Council of India introduced the Legal Education Rules, 2020 , eliminating 1-year LL.M. programs.

Days later, Tamanna Chandan Chanchlani—a holder of a foreign degree—moved the Supreme Court challenging the 2020 Rules, demanding that 1-year LL.M. degrees, whether obtained in India or abroad, be recognised.
While the BCI assured the Court that the changes would not be implemented immediately, the challenge remains pending before the Court.
A Bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi issued notice in the petition on 9 September 2025 , and was later tagged with Upadhyay’s PIL.
On 8 September , the Court flagged the need for appointment of a body of legal experts on legal education, noting that the Union should “ come out with something ” on the matter.
