In contrast, the Wages Code standard of same work or work of a similar nature remains restrictive
in its approach, in assessing the same work or similar nature of work, experience, skill, effort, and responsibility
under Section 2(v), Wages Code would also be considered, but the standard still falls flat as it requires a direct comparison between a woman and man performing an identical or nearly identical work.

Audrey D’Costa4, the Supreme Court of India interpreted Section 4 ERA concerning of same work or work of a similar nature, ruling that the burden of proof is on the employer to show that the work is not similar.
The Wages Code retention of the ERA‘s language implies that the Mackinnon Mackenzie precedent remains valid.
However, without explicit legislative adoption of “equal value”, the judiciary remains the sole avenue for expanding the scope of equal pay, a route often inaccessible to low wage women workers.
The Wages Code does, however, expand protection beyond wages to recruitment.
Section 3 prohibits discrimination on the grounds of sex in recruitment and conditions of employment which ensures continuity with Section 5 ERA.

While the proviso permitting exceptions where employment is “prohibited or restricted by or under any law” remains, while its practical scope should theoretically narrow as the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (OSH&WC Code) replaces blanket prohibitions with regulated safety guarantees.

Further, the Wages Code adds a new protection for women workers provided under Section 29(d), which provides that the employee who is dismissed after being convicted of sexual harassment will not get the statutory bonus benefit.
The OSH&WC Code consolidates laws related to factories, mines, plantations, and contract labour, and fundamentally changed the regulatory landscape for women’s safety and working hours.

Historically, Section 66(1)(b), Factories Act, 1948, had imposed a blanket ban on women working in factories between 7.00 p.m. and 6.00 a.m., this provision was challenged in the R. Vasantha case5, in which the Madras High Court held that Section 66(1)(b) was unconstitutional.
The High Court further held that the protective discrimination cannot be turned into a denial of opportunity and livelihood, and hence, violating Articles 14, 15 and 16.

In 2008, the Supreme Court in Anuj Garg v. Hotel Assn. of India6 reinforced the principle and struck down bans on women who were working in liquor bars, by stating that the State’s incapability to ensure safety cannot be a ground to restrict women’s freedom.

Section 43, OSH&WC Code codifies these judgments by explicitly permitting women workers to work in all establishments for all types of work, including night shifts, subject to the consent of woman, and also provided that it is a duty of the employer to provide adequate safety, working conditions, and safeguards for the women workers concerned.

Generally, the labour market is seen as high unemployment with low bargaining power, in such market the concept of voluntary consent might be risky for women workers, as refusing night shifts might face implicit hiring discrimination or be bypassed for promotions which could hamper the interest for them.7

If we read Section 43, OSH&WC Code, with Rule 73, Draft Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (Central) Rules, 2025 (Draft OSH Rules) then we found that it establishes a baseline for women’s safety during night shifts as it mandates that employers must obtain written consent from women employees and also has to provide adequate transportation facilities for pick-up and drop-off from their residence.

The Draft OSH Rules explicitly mandate for closed-circuit television (CCTV) surveillance near workplace facilities such as washrooms and further mandates for dedicated emergency telephone numbers which must be displayed conspicuously not only at the workplace but also inside the transport vehicles.
The Draft OSH Rules requires not less than three women employees to be on duty at any place for underground mining.
These provisions are robust on paper, but they also add compliance costs which could disincentivise smaller firms from hiring women for night roles.8
The new law replaced old legal ban with a new financial barrier which could impact the interest of women workers.9
Section 2(w), OSH&WC Code raises the threshold for applicability of factories from 10 to 20 workers in factories with power and 20 to 40 workers without power in factories.

This change particularly focuses on the growth of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) by reducing compliance burden, but women workers who are largely concentrated in MSME sector, and particularly in the garment, textile, and food processing sectors.10
By raising the threshold, the OSH&WC Code effectively pushes thousands of small garment units out of the ambit of the factory definition.

Women working in these deregulated units lost their statutory rights of safety committees which is mandatory only for 500+ workers, for canteens which is mandatory for 100+ workers, and for crèches too for which the threshold is 50+ workers.

In industries such as garment manufacturing, where women face risks of byssinosis (lung disease from cotton dust)11 and ergonomic injuries,12 the removal of strict Operational safety oversight for units not falling under the ambit of factory definition under the will lead to significant dilution of health protection.
will lead to significant dilution of health protection.
The Factories Act, 1948, mandated crèches for factories with more than 30 women workers.
The OSH&WC Code modifies this to establishments with 50 or more workers.

While the gender-neutral provision trigger is progressiveness and will acknowledge the male childcare responsibilities, the numeric threshold from 30 to 50 workers allows mid-sized firms to escape the obligation.
Although, the OSH&WC Code introduces the concept of common crèche facilities for class of establishment, allowing firms to pool resources or use State/private facilities within a prescribed distance.
But the problem could arise where the common crèche facility will be far from the establishment where the concerned women work.
The Social Security Code, 2020 consolidates nine laws, aiming to extend social security to the unorganised sector.
Its treatment of maternity benefits and domestic workers offers a study in contrast.
The Social Security Code retains the core provisions of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (as amended in 2017), granting 26 weeks of paid leave for biological mothers.
It formalises benefits for adoptive mothers adopting a child below three months and commissioning mothers for 12 weeks of leave.

The recognition of commissioning mothers aligns with the Delhi High Court’s ruling in Rama Pandey v. Union of India13, which held that a commissioning mother is entitled to maternity leave to bond with the child.
However, the statutory cap of 12 weeks compared to 26 weeks for biological mothers shows a hierarchy of motherhood.
In the Rama Pandey case, the Court emphasised that the need for bonding and care is identical regardless of the biological method of birth.

The 12-week limit in the Social Security Code arguably ignores this judicial reasoning, focusing solely on the physiological recovery of the birth-giving mother rather than the caregiving needs of the child.
Further, the Social Security Code creates a separate category for gig and platform workers, funded by a levy of 1-2 per cent capped at 5 per cent of the aggregator’s turnover.
For women using platforms (for example, beauty services, caregiving apps) this is a significant step towards formalisation.
However, these benefits are scheme-based not statutory rights such as gratuity or PF and solely depend on the government notifying specific schemes.

Also, these benefits will depend on voluntary registration and based on opt-in model, but ILO reports on the informal sectors provides that the voluntary systems would lead to low coverage, unless it falls in mandatory coverage.14
Notable progressive measure provided in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (IR Code), by mandating for gender equity in the Grievance Redressal Committee (hereinafter, “GRC”).

Under Section 4, every establishment employing 20 or more workers must constitute a GRC, the explicit proviso of Section 4(4), that women’s representation therein must be “proportionate” to their strength in the workforce.
This creates a critical separation of powers from the Internal Committee (IC) under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.

While the IC is restricted solely to sexual harassment, Section 4(10), IR Code expressly excludes such matters from the GRC, thereby reserving the GRC for broader individual disputes such as wages, leave, promotions, discriminatory shift allocation, bias in performance appraisals, etc. which ensures that women’s rights at the workplace are recognised beyond the scope of safety.
But the dichotomy remains in the IR Code as it provides the proportionate representation for the women
workers in GRC yet remain silent on women’s representation in work committees.
This dichotomy is nothing but the result for half-baked legislative intent, and path to cover for women workers still remains.

The new Labour Codes have marked a historical shift from a protection-based approach to an enablement-based approach towards women workers by removing blanket restrictions on women’s employment and also strengthen wage security through a uniform wage definition.

New Codes also recognise categories such as commissioning mothers and platform workers which further align with the constitutional principles of equality and also with the judicial rulings that reject paternalistic barriers to women’s right to work.
Although on paper, the Codes are promising greater mobility, formal inclusion, and long-term social security for women workers across sectors.
This shift is kind of double-edged sword, because of which it results in the dilution of enforceable protections.
Many safeguards will now depend on employer consent, future government schemes, or delegated rules, which at some level weakens certainty and access at the ground level.
Increased thresholds under the OSH&WC Code exclude a large number of women working in specifically MSMEs from safety, health, and childcare benefits.
In social security, maternity and platform worker benefits largely remain unequal and highly discretionary.

Long story short, the Codes reflect a continuity in formal equality, they also represent a dilution in guaranteed protection and without strict enforcement, lower thresholds, and conversion of scheme-based benefits into clear statutory rights, the promise of gender justice under the new Labour Codes could only remain symbolic.

Recent developments involving a former SEBI Chairperson, sparked by allegations of undisclosed offshore holdings and potential regulatory lapses, culminating in a Lokpal inquiry, have drawn attention to gaps in the Securities and Exchange Board of India’s (SEBI’s) existing conflicts of interest framework.1
This raised broader questions about the regulator’s ability to safeguard institutional trust.
Possibly as a response to this, SEBI constituted a High-Level Committee (HLC) to review its conflicts of interest framework.2
The HLC submitted its report, which was made public in November 2025.

While the Board has taken cognizance of the recommendations, recent media reports indicate that the proposed framework is likely to be deliberated upon further at the Board’s meeting scheduled for March 2026.
In parallel, the Securities Markets Code Bill, 2025 (SMC) was tabled in Parliament in December 2025.3
This is germane to this discussion because the SMC too, addresses concerns of conflicts of interest at SEBI.

The doctrinal foundation for these design principles is derived from conflicts of interest guidelines articulated by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the World Bank, and the United Nations (UN).4
We identify these principles, and operationalise them through three lines of enquiry, evaluating whether SEBI’s conflicts of interest framework reflects these design principles in practice:

We suggest that making these enquiries and conducting such an analysis can provide a practical way to test whether SEBI’s proposed framework is consistent, balanced, and capable of sustaining public trust.
For each line of enquiry, we identify gaps in SEBI’s conflicts of interest framework, and examine whether the framework proposed by the HLC and the SMC addresses these gaps.
As a measure of SEBI’s international standing on these matters, we study practices from securities regulators in developed-economy jurisdictions on these same three areas.
We use this analysis and comparison to give recommendations for improving SEBI’s conflicts of interest framework, as proposed to be modified by the HLC and the SMC.

SEBI’s organisational structure comprises different types of personnel: Board (Chairperson, and whole-time and part-time members), a full-time professional officer cadre (from Grade A to F), contractual consultants, and support staff.

The framework governing their service conditions and ethical conduct is defined by two documents: the SEBI (Employees’ Service) Regulations, 2001 (the “Regulations”),5 and the SEBI Code on Conflicts of Interest for Board Members, 2008 (the “Code”).6
The Regulations and the Code set standards for disclosure and conduct, which form the basis of the regulator’s ethics policy.
They also spell out other terms, such as pay and post-employment restrictions.

This question is rooted in the principle that governance at regulators must be transparent,7 and that institutions must have risk management systems for oversight of disclosure and conflict avoidance.8
Mandatory disclosures of interests and personal accountability become critical in ensuring this.
With this in mind, we assess how role-based differentiation is structured in SEBI’s disclosure framework.
SEBI’s disclosure framework imposes varying requirements on personnel based on their role and seniority.
While the Regulations are only applicable to full-time employees, the Code is applicable only to the Board.
It is important to note here that there are no codified rules for disclosures by part-time employees and consultants.

This gap means that consultants and part-time employees (PTMs) such as data analysts, cyber forensic and derivatives experts, etc. who may have access to sensitive information, are left outside the framework entirely.
Notably, in FY 2024-2025, SEBI’s Board comprised five PTMs alongside the Chairperson and four whole-time members (WTMs).9
Collectively, these five PTMs were invited to 17 Board meetings during their respective tenures, and attended 11 of them.
Neither the Regulations nor the Code explicitly provide a definition of “conflicts of interest”.
This creates ambiguity about what constitutes a conflict and how it should be identified and managed.

Further, the definition of “family” is critical because disclosure obligations and investment restrictions are triggered not only by the employee’s own trades, but also by those of their “family” members, making the scope of this term central to the reach of the framework.
An inconsistency in defining “family” creates an opportunity for employees to channel trades through relatives and thereby evade disclosure requirements.

Notably, the Regulations adopt a broader definition of “family” that includes spouses, dependent children and stepchildren, and any persons wholly dependent on the employee through blood or marriage.10
On the other hand, the Code restricts the meaning of “family” to include only spouses and children under 18.11

No Explanation is available for why different definitions are adopted across the Regulations and the Code, nor for why Board Members are held to a lower standard of accountability than rank-and-file employees.
Additionally, the Regulations stipulate sanctions for any compliance failures.
The sanctions can be classified as either “minor” (withholding promotions, recovery of pecuniary loss), and “major” (reduced pay, compulsory retirement, dismissal).
These sanctions are not related to the role or seniority of the violator.
The Code, on the other hand, does not outline sanctions for violations.12
The HLC has integrated the Code and the Regulations into a single framework.
However, it has carried forward the two-tier structure by not fully extending the framework to PTMs.
PTMs participate in regulatory decision-making, and access price-sensitive information, both of which influence market structure.
By not subjecting them to equivalent disclosure and investment restriction requirements, the framework leaves out a material blind spot.
Further, the proposed definition of “conflicts of interest” defines a conflict by way of its effect rather than specifying what constitutes a conflict.
While the HLC’s supplemental classification (financial, relational, professional, fiduciary, and perceived) provides guidance, it shifts the burden onto personnel to identify and disclose conflicts.
This introduces substantial subjectivity.
For instance, one could claim that a financial interest “did not actually influence” their impartiality, leaving enforcement dependent on interpretation.
The HLC has proposed to revise the definition of “family” to include persons related by blood or marriage, who are “substantially dependent” on the employee.
However, it does not define “substantially”.
At the same time, it proposes adopting the broader definition of “relative” from the Companies Act, 2013 for disclosure and recusal, and not for investment restrictions.

Investment restrictions continue to apply only to the narrower “family” category, meaning that non-dependent relatives, such as siblings or parents may still trade in restricted securities, provided the relationship is disclosed.
Lastly, neither the HLC nor the SMC, proposes a clear and proportionate sanctions structure.
Instead, they rely on removal from office and “appropriate action”.
While the HLC states that non-disclosure or non-recusal should attract action, it does not define intermediate penalties or what “appropriate action” means.
If removal is the only sanction, it is unlikely to be used for moderate lapses.

Unlike SEBI, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in the US and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) in the UK, apply a uniform baseline of disclosure requirements to all personnel and then layer on stricter restrictions in line with seniority.
For instance, the SEC applies its conflicts of interest and disclosure rules to all personnel, including secondees and contractors, with a stringency that escalates by role.
Similarly, the FCA extends its disclosure rules to all categories of staff, including fixed-term employees, contractors, secondees, and agency workers.

(a) To define “family”, a risk-based approach could be adopted, restricting the definition to spouse, dependent children under 18, and wholly dependent individuals, while retaining the flexibility to cover a wider circle of relatives for Board Members, in specific sensitive positions.
A limited formulation on violation of the disclosure framework weakens the Code’s deterrent effect.

To address this gap, the new framework should: 1) establish uniform sanctions that apply to all personnel for basic disclosure violations; and 2) introduce a system of differentiated sanctions linked to seniority.

Under such a system, the same breach could attract progressively stricter penalties as the rank and responsibility of the personnel increases, recognising that lapses from Board Members carry higher institutional risks, and they are held to higher standards of accountability.
We frame this question in the context of the principle that public interest is at the core of institutional integrity.13
This requires employees of public institutions to separate their private interests from their public duties.
Where conflicts arise, they should either dispose of such interests or recuse themselves from related decisions.
Officers in roles especially prone to conflicts of interest must follow stricter protocols proportionate to the risks they face.
Against this backdrop, we examine investment-related restrictions under SEBI’s disclosure framework.

The Regulations impose a near-total ban on employees from making any direct or indirect investment in equity, equity-related instruments, and commodity derivatives, with limited and specific exceptions for units of mutual funds and non-convertible bonds.14
This prohibition extends to family members when the investments are funded by the employee or made on their behalf.
In contrast, the Code only requires that Board Members disclose their and their family’s shareholdings, and that WTMs disclose “substantial transactions” by themselves and their family.15

This suggests that holding and transacting in shares is permissible for the Board, but not for employees governed by the Regulations, which place a general prohibition on equity and equity-related investments.

The reason for this differentiation is unclear; and while safeguards on those with access to market-sensitive information are necessary, a complete bar may disincentivise many from considering employment with the regulator.
Disparity in investment restrictions between employees and the Board (barring PTMs) has been eliminated.
The Board is now barred from dealing in direct equities, matching the rules applicable to employees.
Both categories are instead permitted to invest in professionally managed pooled vehicles, provided that investments with a single intermediary do not exceed 25 per cent of their financial portfolio.
Pooled vehicles (e.g., mutual funds) are highly diversified instruments where investors have no control over selection of securities.

The 25 per cent concentration cap forces all personnel to split investments across multiple asset managers and continuously monitor portfolio values to avoid any inadvertent breach due to regular market movements.
Further, mutual fund returns depend on underlying securities, not the profitability of the asset manager.
This change increases compliance burdens and is not solving for a real ethical risk.
The abovementioned equity trading ban has been extended to the spouses of all personnel.
While aimed at preventing indirect conflicts, this treats the spouses merely as extensions and restricts their financial agency.
This treats the spouses of junior HR or IT employees exactly the same as the spouse of the SEBI Chairperson.
In contrast, a non-dependent parent, sibling, or adult child of a SEBI Board Member is permitted to trade in equities (as long as the relationship is disclosed).
The HLC has rejected the “blind-trust” investment route.
Now, upon joining WTMs must liquidate, freeze, or sell (according to a pre-declared trading plan) their existing portfolios.
This restriction might deter private sector experts from joining and compromise SEBI’s competence.
The SEC and the FCA permit their employees to invest in equities, but impose strict prohibitions on high-risk activities.
Specifically, the SEC prohibits short selling, margin trading, investments in its directly regulated entities and in IPOs.16
More importantly, employees may use the blind trust construct to manage conflicts.

Therein, a filer does not need to report specific holdings or income from a qualified blind or diversified trust; instead, disclosure is limited to aggregate income categories for the filer, spouse, or dependent child.17
On the other hand, the FCA bans speculative transactions and direct dealings in securities of FCA regulated firms.18
Permit limited, low-risk market participation for all personnel, while simultaneously applying restrictions based on a personnel’s role sensitivity.
Under such a system, direct investments in non-regulated entities, for e.g., any private company, could be allowed; since they are not regulated by SEBI.
Subject high-risk or sensitive investments to prior approval, while allowing lower value investments to proceed without pre-clearance.
Here, SEBI should also introduce specific numeric thresholds to clearly distinguish between high-risk and low-risk investments.

We now examine SEBI’s post-employment restrictions in the context of the principle that public institutions must have systems for comprehensive management and oversight of disclosure and conflict avoidance regimes.19
Such measures must provide for timely identification of “at-risk” activities and the adoption of suitable preventive measures.
Methods such as divestment, recusal, or resignation, and re-arranging duties where necessary can be used in this regard.
In this context, we specifically examine SEBI’s framework on post-employment restrictions.
For all employees, the stipulated post-employment restriction period in the Regulations is one year from the date they “finally cease to be in the Board’s service”.
Specifically, the Regulations provide that for a year after leaving SEBI, a former employee must seek approval from the competent authority20 before:

1) taking up a commercial engagement (for example, offering private consultancy in areas where employees have gained insider knowledge or engaging in liaison work with SEBI); or 2) “associating with” a SEBI-registered intermediary.
Interestingly, the Code does not envision any post-employment restrictions for the Board.
Further, the effectiveness of these restrictions on employees is undermined by a key ambiguity: the term “associated with” in the context of SEBI-registered intermediaries is not defined.
This may prevent SEBI from clearly identifying and monitoring prohibited relationships with intermediaries.

The SMC mandates that for one year after demitting office, a Board Member cannot accept employment with any securities markets service provider, market participant or any other person associated with securities markets.
They cannot appear before or against SEBI in any recognition, adjudication, settlement, or approval matter for a period of two years from their date of retirement or relief.
This also extends to contractual employees, consultants, and advisors.
The SEC’s post-employment framework imposes a permanent ban on former employees from representing external parties in matters they directly worked on during their tenure.

In addition, senior employees are subject to a one-year “cooling-off” communication ban, under which they may not contact or communicate with the SEC on behalf of another person or entity about specific matters they were involved with while at the SEC.21
By contrast, the FCA has a more flexible and individualised approach.
Rather than imposing a blanket ban, the FCA’s post-employment policy is based on a case-by-case assessment of potential conflicts.
Former officials are required to complete mandatory forms, which are reviewed to determine if their new role poses any risk.22
We recommend that while a full one-year ban must continue to apply to all Board Members, certain modifications could be made to the uniform one-year post-employment ban applicable to all personnel:

On three key questions, we critically examined the existing framework, and conducted a comparative study of leading international agencies such as the OECD and the World Bank, and regulators like the SEC and FCA.

Our recommendations employ insights from these comparisons, and emphasise adopting a tiered approach to disclosures, easing investment restrictions for junior personnel in non-sensitive roles, and implementing a risk-based assessment for post-employment restrictions for all personnel.
We suggest that SEBI’s conflicts of interest framework needs changes to address gaps and inconsistencies, and to bring it in line with prevailing international standards.
This need for change is based on the requirements of consistency and comprehensiveness.
An inconsistent policy, even if well-intentioned, creates regulatory gaps and undermines public trust.
Vague definitions and the absence of uniform standards leave room for loopholes and weaken institutional credibility.

SEBI’s revised conflicts of interest framework, therefore, must be anchored in clear, consistent, and proportionate standards to safeguard effective market governance without compromising on institutional integrity.

In India, Phase III of E-Courts Project has included a component of AI to enhance case management and legal research.
It has a component for future technological advancement, including AI and blockchain, across the High Courts in India up to 2027 with separate budget outlay.
Judicial work is, and always has been, synonymous with application of mind.
A Judge, as his core function, marshals the facts and appreciates the evidence presented before him.
After applying law on such facts and evidence, a judgment is written with reasons supporting the conclusion.
Reasons are the heart and soul of a judicial order.
Lack of such reasons makes a decision arbitrary and betrays the most important essential of judicial determination.
The advent of artificial intelligence (AI), despite its several positives, threatens the application of human mind in passing such reasoned judgments.1
Judiciaries, across the world, are arriving at an inflection point where judges resort to AI chatbots for their research and drafting.2
It is only a short step from there to using AI to generate judgments.

The Chief Justice of India had recently assured that AI will not be used in judicial decision-making and held that “independence and human discretion of judges remain central to the Indian justice system”.3
However, the prospect of AI being used by judges looms.
Judges may resort to it to reduce their excessive burden and give in to the convenience that it provides.
When presented with facts and evidence, AI systems generate a reasoned judgment with a discussion of all such facts and evidence.4
They create efficiency and help oil the judicial machinery to enable it to dispense faster justice.
But the ostensible efficiency creates several problems.
In this article, we discuss the threats that emanate from the use of AI and its slippery slope which may lead the judges to use AI systems for decision-making.
While it is true that AI creates convenience and efficiency in judicial functions, its use has to be guided with human control and accountability.
It may appear that this is an argument against convenience, but using AI cautiously will ensure that such convenience does not undermine reasoning and propriety of a judicial decision.
When such use is unguided, there is a threat of orders and judgments being passed without sufficient supervision to check the veracity of the legal positions contained in them.
AI systems work by analysing large amounts of data to identify patterns and relationships.5
Based on these patterns, they produce responses or predictions to new inputs, rather than reasoning in a human and value-based manner.6
As a result, their outputs are shaped by the data on which they are trained and the limits built into their design.
Their response, however, is not parallel to human reasoning.7
They try to mimic human reasoning based on all the information they have as to how earlier decisions have been taken.
While, there are general AI systems such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Grok, there have been specific systems developed for the legal field.
Lucio AI is used by lawyers across the world for their legal research and drafting assistance.
Harvey AI is specifically targeted at law firms with transactional practice.
Spellbook helps draft contracts and Kira Systems does contract review and due diligence for mergers and acquisitions.
Even judiciaries across the world have started developing AI systems intended to be used by their judges.
Germany has developed OLGA to categorise cases and extract relevant case data.8
Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS) is a system used in some parts of the United States for sentencing guidance.9
In British Columbia, Canada, a system called the “Solution Explorer” guides the litigants in the pre-trial phase by estimating their chances of success if they approach the courts.10
China has built a similar system called “Xiao Fa”.11
The most ambitious of them all is Victor, a system being developed by Brazil.
Victor is built on a convolutional neural network (CNN).
A CNN is a type of artificial neural network commonly used to analyse images and, in some cases, to process and understand language.12
According to its developers, Victor does not make decisions on its own but merely assists court clerks in sorting and screening appeals.13

However, there is scepticism around this as it is argued that it is difficult to draw a clear line between human decision-making and the subtle influence that software tools can exert on human reasoning.14
In India, Phase III of E-Courts Project has included a component of AI to enhance case management and legal research.
It has a component for future technological advancement, including AI and blockchain, across the High Courts in India up to 2027 with separate budget outlay.15

It includes intelligent scheduling of cases, case prediction to enable the parties predict probable outcomes of their case, natural language processing for legal research and translation of documents, and data security measures.16
This complements the already existing tools such as Adalat AI which transcribes court proceedings such as witness depositions and oral arguments.17

Further, an AI-based software tool called Legal Research Analysis Assistant (LegRAA) has been developed to aid judges in legal research and document analysis, but is yet to be adopted by judges in their routine work.18

Another tool called Supreme Court Portal for Assistance in Court’s Efficiency (SUPACE) has been created to aid judges by retrieving facts from documents submitted by the litigants and providing relevant case laws.19
However, its adoption has been limited as it is only used for criminal matters before the Delhi and Bombay High Courts.
While these initiatives are undoubtedly welcome, they require careful and cautious engagement.
There is little dispute that AI can enhance efficiency and accelerate the disposal of cases in trial courts.
Yet, this very promise compels a deeper inquiry into its limits.
To what extent should AI be permitted to operate within the judicial process?
What happens when systems designed for assistance begin to be used beyond their intended scope?
And how does the legitimacy of adjudication fare if judges increasingly rely on AI for decision-making rather than independent judicial reasoning?
Most importantly, why is human reasoning better than reasoning supplied by AI in drafting orders and judgments?
These questions must be answered before AI is routinely used by the trial courts judges.
Adjudication in trial courts is fact-heavy and fact-specific.
Merely because two cases have similar facts, the result cannot be the same.
A large language model learns from the vast data available on the internet and responds by identifying similarities.20
This can create a problem of generalisation even though the specific facts at hand deserve an independent deliberation.21

For example, when it encounters an interlocutory application for temporary injunction that appears similar to another application found on the internet, it may treat both of them as identical and suggest the same outcome.
Hence, if the petition found on the internet was allowed, the model is likely to recommend allowance of the subsequent one as well.
However, pleadings may be superficially similar while the underlying facts and surrounding circumstances differ materially.
Judicial determination requires each factual situation to be assessed independently, without mechanical reliance on precedent or pattern.
The use of AI in such contexts therefore risks undermining such application of independent judicial mind, which is a core foundation of adjudication.
To ensure that each case is decided on its own merits, the documentary evidence produced during the trial of such case has to be perused.
A significant concern arises when AI systems are expected to extract and evaluate facts from such documents, a task that lies at the very core of a trial Judge’s function.

Judges are required to peruse a wide and often unstructured range of documents, ranging from panchanamas to land records maintained in regional languages, such as Pahanis or Adangals in Telugu-speaking States.
In many instances, these documents are handwritten, poorly preserved, or contain overwriting, corrections, and interpolations.
An AI system may struggle not only to accurately extract data from such records, but also to comprehend their legal significance.
Optical character recognition (OCR) using AI is not foolproof and is susceptible to errors arising from document quality, formatting, and language complexity.22
Even where extraction is attempted, a deeper question arises as to whether the system can correctly contextualise those facts in relation to the issue under consideration.
Corrections in documents, or explanations
offered during oral evidence, such as an investigating officer clarifying the absence of date in an inquest panchanama, require careful human evaluation.
Further, a substantial portion of judicial records in India are not machine-readable.23
The assessment of their probative value necessarily demands independent application of the human mind, which cannot be delegated to AI systems.24
When an order or a judgment is generated using AI system, the Judge is not articulating his reasoning behind the decision.
Rather, he is merely confirming the reasoning stated by the AI system.
This converts the job of a judge from “application of mind” to produce a well-reasoned result to “confirmation of output” of the AI.
Hence, instead of constructing the reason, a judge is simply auditing the reason.
If such reason is well-articulated, a judge may find it compelling to approve it, rather than take the efforts to finding any flaws to correct such reasoning before pronouncing the judgment.25
When this becomes routine, the intensity of how minutely the reason is reviewed gradually diminishes.
It betrays the essential feature of a judicial function which is to decide by the application of human mind.26
This will lead to a creation of “black box” where one is unable to ascertain why an AI system has produced an order in a particular manner.27

Some have argued that a judges should be provided with a dedicated AI tool, called “Explainable AI” which also explains the reasons behind a determination made by it, and until such time, judges should be restricted to delegate their reasoning functions to an AI system.28
As the output of AI barely takes any time, a judge may not dedicate several hours needed to peruse through the evidence with an open mind and find out if the losing side has any strength in its case.
It is often seen that a doubt created during dictation of a judgment leads a judge to ponder on whether such judgment is going on the right track.
However, AI does not provide any such opportunity as it cuts shorts the efforts of the judge to take a deep dive into the evidence.

It is for this reason that the House of Lords stated in its Select Committee Report that “it is not acceptable to deploy any artificial intelligence system which could have a substantial impact on an individual’s life, unless it can generate a full and satisfactory explanation for the decisions it will take”.29
When it becomes public knowledge that a judge uses AI systems to produce his orders or judgments, it casts a blow to public trust in judiciary.
It erodes trust in the judicial system where human reasoning is expected to be applied.
This undermines the prestige of the judiciary as it will seem that the core judicial function has been outsourced to a computer software.30
This also provides a new ground for appeal where a new wave of appeals may be preferred on the ground that the judgment of the trial court was not written by the Judge himself, but by an AI system.
A fundamental ethical concern arises as the process risks diluting accountability and the moral responsibility that lies at the heart of adjudication.
The European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, 2024, adopts a risk-based regulatory framework that classifies AI activities into four categories: banned, high-risk, limited risk, and minimal risk.31
Notably, the deployment of AI for legal research, interpretative assistance, and the application of law to facts is designated as “high-risk”.

Reflecting the sensitivity of adjudicatory functions, the Act mandates meaningful human oversight wherever AI is used within judicial processes, underscoring that technology may assist but cannot supplant human judgment.

There is no such requirement in India, and even when such requirement is enacted as a law or mandated by rules of practice, ensuring that there is adequate human oversight to not undermine application of mind by the judges is difficult.

The Delhi High Court sounded this alarm when it held that “there is no doubt in the mind of the court that, at the present stage of technological development, AI cannot substitute either human intelligence or the humane element in the adjudicatory process. At best, the tool could be utilised for preliminary understanding or for preliminary research, and nothing more.”32

Another serious ethical concern arises when trial courts rely on AI-generated legal research, as such systems may fabricate authorities and reinforce the user’s pre-existing belief rather than accurately stating the law.
At times, AI software “hallucinates” case law by creating fictitious judgments that appear plausible and authoritative and presents them confidently to affirm what the user seeks.33
Upon verification on authentic legal databases such as SCC, these cases are found not to exist at all.
Such “ghost” case law grossly misrepresents legal principles, and if relied upon by trial courts, may result in orders based on non-existent decisions of the Supreme Court or High Courts.
To illustrate this, consider the following prompt that was inserted by the authors on ChatGPT:
This case involved a dispute over the vast estate of late industrialist Priyamvada Birla.
There was a will, and parties were fighting over its validity.
One side sought appointment of a receiver to protect the estate from being misused during litigation.

“Appointment of a receiver is a drastic and harsh remedy and should be exercised with extreme caution and only when there is a strong prima facie case and a clear danger of loss or damage to the property in dispute.“
In the entire reply above, the only thing that ChatGPT got right is the case name and its citation.
However, when we traced this case from SCC OnLine, it was found that the case does not talk about receiver at all.
It is a case law on several legal principles of probate.
When ChatGPT is questioned further, it conveniently acknowledges it and backtracks from its earlier response, as seen here:
The exact quote you’re referring to — that “appointment of a receiver is a drastic and harsh remedy and should be exercised with extreme caution…” — does not appear verbatim in Krishna Kumar Birla v.
I couldn’t locate that precise language in the available judgment text.
It seems that your earlier citation is more of a paraphrase or legal commentary summarizing the spirit of the decision rather than a literal excerpt.

This kind of phraseology—“drastic remedy,” “strong prima facie case,” and “real danger”—is commonly attributed to judicial reasoning around receivership, but it isn’t present word-for-word in the Supreme Court’s written decision in that case.
If you want a literal judicial statement from an opinion, we’d have to turn to another case where those exact words were used.
Want me to look up an alternative judgment with that precise phrasing?
There have been several instances across the world where courts and lawyers have relied on such non-existent case laws.34
In the year 2024, a trial Judge in Brazil unwittingly endorsed a draft order prepared by a court clerk who had used ChatGPT to generate portions of the reasoning without disclosing this fact.35
Relying on the authorities cited in the draft, the Judge incorporated case law that later turned out to be fictitious and factually incorrect.
This led to a wrongful conviction of the accused.36
This not only betrays the trust of litigants but also places a significant burden on appellate and Revisional Courts to correct errors that should never have arisen.
A cautionary example is the widely reported incident in New York, where two lawyers were debarred after filing pleadings supported by AI-generated false citations.37
Further, even where AI systems cite real case law, such decisions may be outdated, overruled, or rendered inapplicable by subsequent legal developments.38
The reliability of AI output is directly linked to the scope, depth, and currency of the legal material it is permitted to access.

Where an AI system operates under informational or database limitations, it is far more likely to produce defective responses grounded in incorrect or obsolete positions of law, thereby raising profound ethical and institutional concerns for judicial decision-making.
The Delhi High Court had dismissed a petition as withdrawn when it found that a petition contained several fake case laws and cited text which did not exist in the case laws.39
A dilemma arises when trial courts rely on AI systems trained on skewed legal datasets, as such dependence may distort judicial discretion and outcomes.
Most of the legal material accessible to AI systems consists of judgments of the Supreme Court and the High Courts in India since these decisions are readily available online.
However, the matters that reach higher courts are themselves not representative of all judicial outcomes.40
For instance, an order granting bail at the trial court level is seldom challenged, whereas an order refusing bail is far more likely to be carried in appeal or revision.
As a result, higher court decisions disproportionately contain discussions on when and why bail should be granted and the parameters governing such grant.

When a trial court Judge relies on AI assistance to draft or decide bail applications, the system which learns from the Supreme Court and the High Court orders may incline towards allowing bail rather than refusing it.

While this tendency may appear to favour the constitutional value of personal liberty, the same bias can become problematic in other contexts, where there are special legislations governing grant of bail such as offences relating to narcotic drugs or when police seek custody of an accused, where mechanically allowing petitions without human application of mind may itself amount to an affront to liberty and public interest.
A grave concern arises when AI systems internalise and reproduce deep-seated societal prejudices, thereby threatening the constitutional promise of equality before law.

A decision by the Supreme Court of Wisconsin in the United States has been often cited to show how algorithmic decision-making, when trained on socially skewed data, can amplify existing inequalities under the guise of objectivity.41
In State of Wisconsin v. Loomis (2016), the Supreme Court of Wisconsin upheld the use of a risk-assessment algorithm, called COMPAS, at the sentencing stage to evaluate the likelihood of recidivism.
While approving its use, the Court expressly cautioned trial courts that such tools are susceptible to bias against marginalised communities, particularly the Black population in the United States.42
Empirical studies revealed that Black individuals were classified as likely to reoffend at nearly twice the rate of white individuals by software such as COMPAS.43

A similar danger exists in the Indian context, where AI systems, if trained on data reflecting entrenched social hierarchies, may unfairly disadvantage lower castes and religious minorities, thereby institutionalising discrimination through automated judicial assistance.44
Such pattern recognition may be used by the AI system to also find if a judge has any particular inclination and help the litigants and lawyers with forum shopping.45
Hence, an AI system may read the judgments delivered by a Judge of the Supreme Court or the High Court and label a Judge to be “pro-landlord” or “pro-tenant”.
This leads to predictive analysis where the lawyers will aim to get their matter called before a judge who is likely to be favourable to their case.
Software such as Lex Machina46 in the United States or Solomonic47 in the United Kingdom have already started type casting judges on such lines.
When such label is attached to a judge, it erodes public confidence in objectivity of justice system.
When the AI systems are used regularly, they may tend to diminish the judicial skills of judges which was harnessed by training at Judicial Academies and experience gained by them over the years.
This leads to “cognitive offloading” where judges surrender their judicial skills to AI which may diminish their abilities of critical thinking.48
The judgments are made to look good as they are drafted by the AI to seem more structured and nuanced, which improves their readability and may make them easier to understand even by non-law persons.
However, this verbosity may betray the actual application of judicial mind.
Judges may start paying less attention to the oral arguments of the counsel as the pleadings and evidence would be sufficient for AI to generate a judgment.
Ultimately, judgments of all judges will look alike and become standardised, undermining the diversity and style that each Judge may have.

This homogenised language erodes judicial individuality, something that makes us appreciate the writings of stalwart Judges such as Justice Krishna Iyer or Justice K.T. Thomas, who are well-known for their linguistic flair and analytical articulation.

While it is not desirable for a trial court Judge to draft judgments in complicated language, it is also not prudent to allow all judgments to be standardised as it may betray organic reasoning that a judge is likely to articulate when a judgment is written by him.49
At a moral level, judges would be delegating the job they are entrusted with to a computer software, and this may have significant repercussions in the long-run.50
A litigant may question if his case was adjudged by a human judge or simply processed by a software.
The elements of equity, beyond the concept of strict justice, will become blurred.

The danger of AI in judging is not that machines will replace judges, but that judges may slowly begin to think like machines as they optimise, standardise, and minimise risk at the cost of conscience.51
AI may increase efficiency as a managerial value, but justice is a moral enterprise which needs to be preserved.
Judicial reasoning is not merely the mechanical application of rules to facts.
It is a deliberative process shaped by constitutional values, moral intuition, and institutional responsibility.52
A human judge does not simply match fact patterns to precedents but evaluates them through empathy, proportionality, and an awareness of consequences.
This distinction becomes evident in concrete situations.
Consider a bail application in a criminal case.
Two accused persons may face identical charges under the same statutory provision.
An AI system trained on past data may detect that bail is frequently denied in such offences and suggest refusal.53
A human judge, however, may notice that one accused is a first-time offender, the sole caregiver of an ailing parent, and has cooperated with investigation.
The Judge weighs liberty under Article 21, the absence of flight risk, and the proportionality of continued incarceration.
What changes the outcome is not statistical similarity but contextual humanity.
Even in sentencing, where structured guidelines exist, human reasoning plays a transformative role.
Two offenders convicted of the same offence may differ radically in remorse, background, and prospects of reform.
A judge may perceive genuine contrition in an apology, or insincerity masked by rehearsed words.
AI can analyse language patterns, but it cannot experience moral resonance or detect authenticity in the human sense.54
In a civil injunction matter, a machine might treat delay in filing as a decisive factor against relief.
A judge may instead examine why the delay occurred: illiteracy, rural disadvantage, misinformation, or economic vulnerability.
Equity often demands sensitivity to structural inequality, something that cannot be statistically inferred with moral certainty.
Similarly, in a family dispute involving custody, AI may identify common judicial language about the “best interest of the child”.

Yet the lived assessment of a judge which involves observing the child’s interaction with each parent, perceiving emotional cues in court, sensing manipulation or genuine affection cannot be reduced to textual inputs.
Judicial reasoning here is experiential, not algorithmic.
AI operates through probabilistic pattern recognition.
It can organise, summarise, and correlate data, but it does not understand suffering, intention, remorse, fear, or dignity.
Yet doubt is central to judging: the hesitation before conviction, the second reading of evidence before dismissal, the conscious discomfort that leads to re-examination of a harsh conclusion.55
Human reasoning permits reconsideration, while algorithmic output tends toward premature finality.56
The courts derive authority not merely from efficiency or consistency, but from the assurance that decisions are made by accountable human minds exercising independent judgment.
In a constitutional democracy, judging is not optimisation, it is responsibility.
AI, if carefully confined to a purely assistive role, can be legitimately used by trial court Judges to support the process of adjudication without intruding into decision-making.57

AI may be employed for tasks such as transcribing evidence, summarising pleadings and depositions, organising case records, translating documents, and rectifying spelling and grammatical mistakes in the orders drafted by the judges.

Used in this manner, AI functions as an advanced clerical and research aid which reduces mechanical workload, saves judicial time, and improves administrative efficiency, while the core judicial functions of appreciating evidence, weighing competing arguments, applying discretion, and delivering reasoned conclusions remain firmly and exclusively with the judge.58
In short, AI may assist the judge’s hands, but must never substitute the judge’s mind.
Institutions across the world have reacted to the advent of AI by framing guidelines to define their approach.
United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) has issued a document containing fifteen principles regarding the use of AI in the trial courts.59
They emphasise that AI in courts must remain human-centred, rights-respecting, transparent, and accountable, with strong safeguards against bias, discrimination, and opacity.60

In the context of trial courts, these principles require that AI be used only as an assistive tool, with judges retaining full control, responsibility, and discretion over every judicial decision, while ensuring fairness, explainability, and protection of human dignity.61

Similarly, the European Union has adopted an “Ethical Charter on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Systems and their Environment” which stipulates that AI must remain strictly subordinate to human judges, and must never undermine judicial independence or discretion.62
It mandates transparency, non-discrimination, and effective human control, affirming that the act of judging is a human function that cannot be delegated to algorithms.
On the other hand, France has enacted a law specifically prohibiting the use of AI to predict decisions of an individual judge based on his past judgments.63
In India, the Kerala High Court has formulated a policy titled “the policy regarding use of artificial intelligence tools in district judiciary”.64

At the outset, it makes a distinction between “AI tools” and “approved AI tools”, the latter being tools which have “undergone formal evaluation and received approval from the Kerala High Court or the Supreme Court of India for use at the District Judiciary”.65

It lays down unequivocally that “AI tools shall not be used to arrive at any findings, reliefs, order or judgment under any circumstances as the responsibility for the content and integrity of the judicial order, judgment or any part thereof lies fully with the Judges”.66
It warns its judicial officers not to compromise transparency, fairness, accountability, and confidentiality, which are integral aspects of judiciary.67
Hence, specific information regarding the litigants and their disputes should not be uploaded to any AI tool as it may use this information, resulting in breach of privacy.68
Further, it recognises that AI produces “erroneous, incomplete, or biased results” and extreme caution must be exercised in relying on the citations and legal position suggested by such AI tools.69

It proposes and encourages its officers to participate in training programs organised by the High Court or the Judicial Academy to understand the ethical, legal, technical and practical aspects of AI.70

Although some have taken objection to the application of the policy of the Kerala High Court only to the district judiciary, exempting the High Court itself,71 a policy of such nature is indeed a welcome move.
It is only fitting that other High Courts across the country create such policies and give guidance to their respective judicial officers.
The judiciaries across the States in India, headed by their High Courts and guided by the Supreme Court, must deal with the use of AI proactively.
Akin to the policy of the Kerala High Court, other High Courts must also frame policy and guidelines for their judges.
Distinction must be made to mandate what is permissible and non-permissible use of AI.
It must be made abundantly clear that AI is not to be used as a replacement of human application of mind.
This “red line” must be drawn to protect judicial integrity and accountability in the orders passed and judgments pronounced.
AI tools are merely assistive, and a “human-in-the-loop” principle must be followed by all judicial officers to apply their minds independently.
Predictive analysis is required to be governed to avoid any likelihood of forum shopping.
It can be used, however, to predict an outcome which may nudge the parties to arrive at a mediated settlement.
A National Judicial AI Oversight Committee, or a sub-committee under the umbrella of e-Committee, may be created by the Supreme Court to oversee and guide the use of AI tools in the country.
This Committee can formulate policies, conduct seminars, and prescribe sensitisation and skill enhancement training to all judicial officers in the country.
Such unified national approach will avoid fragmented measures across the country at the State-level.72
The High Courts and the State Judicial Academies need to design training programs to improve abilities of judges in using AI tools and demonstrate both good and bad uses of the same.
A hands-on approach can be used in such training programs to show the pitfalls of AI tools, especially in using such tools for legal research.
It is also important that ethical values be inculcated amongst judges as a part of AI literacy.
The judiciaries across the country must aim at preventing dependency of judges on AI tools.
Judgments written by the trial court Judges must be regularly reviewed to ensure that there are no fictitious case laws or that AI tools have not been used for reasoned orders.

Ultimately, the judicial responsibility of every order passed and judgment written must rest solely with the judge, and it cannot be shifted to any AI tool irrespective of the efficiency of such AI tool.
AI can modernise court administration, but adjudication is not an administrative function, it is a constitutional trust.

The Supreme Court and High Courts must therefore act not merely as adopters of technology, but as guardians of the human character of justice, ensuring that AI remains a tool of assistance, not an instrument of substitution.
